title: Sequoia, Tiger Global Circle Kalshi in Fresh $1B Funding Talks: Report
content:
The company’s valuation history tells quite a story. In October 2025, Kalshi raised $300 million at a $5 billion valuation before securing another $1 billion in December at an $11 billion valuation. By May 2026, the company had collected another $1 billion, doubling its valuation to $22 billion. Now, just four months later, the report says Kalshi is negotiating yet another billion-dollar financing round that would put its valuation at approximately $40 billion.
The proposed valuation represents a 700% increase from October’s figure, and the latest negotiations arrive before Kalshi has even completed a full year since its $5 billion benchmark. The transaction remains unconfirmed, however, and neither the final investor lineup nor the closing date has been announced.
A Prediction Market With Traditional Exchange Ambitions
Founded in 2018 by Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, Kalshi operates a federally regulated marketplace where traders buy contracts that pay based on whether particular events happen. Its growth has been substantial. Company figures released in May showed annualized trading volume climbing from $52 billion to $178 billion over six months, while institutional volume increased 800%.
Kalshi is now courting hedge funds, insurers, and asset managers, developing institutional trading products while positioning itself against established exchange operators such as CME Group and Intercontinental Exchange (ICE). Alongside this, ICE has its own relationship with Polymarket. Kalshi rival Polymarket is reportedly negotiating its own billion-dollar financing, with earlier reporting pointing to a valuation exceeding $20 billion.
A $40 Billion Price Tag Meets a State Gambling Fight
There’s a complication behind those impressive valuations. On Sept. 25, the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against Kalshi in litigation involving Ohio and Tennessee, allowing those states to regulate their respective sports contracts under gambling laws.
Kalshi maintains that its federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) oversight governs the products and has challenged the ruling’s legal durability. Trump’s CFTC agrees with this stance and has met state regulators in court. The dispute creates an intriguing contradiction. Investors are discussing an eightfold valuation increase for a company whose sports contracts, a major source of trading activity, remain contested by state regulators in several jurisdictions.
Kalshi has also held preliminary discussions about going public, although Mansour previously indicated that an initial public offering (IPO) wasn’t planned for 2026. For now, the $40 billion figure is still a negotiating target. The company is seeking another billion dollars while the state courts continue debating precisely what kind of business it is.

title: Circle Stock Near $91; Binance and Tazapay Deals Highlight Share-Issuance Mechanics
content:
Circle has already issued Binance 1,237,011 Class A shares for a $100 million investment at a fixed price of $80.84 per share. The Tazapay transaction differs because its final share count has not yet been set.
Under the Tazapay purchase agreement, the initial closing share issuance will be based on an Estimated Purchase Price and CRCL’s volume-weighted average closing price over the 20 trading days immediately before closing. The agreement then provides for a post-closing purchase-price true-up: a downward adjustment can be satisfied by cancelling shares in the indemnity holdback reserve or transferring them out of that reserve. An upward adjustment requires additional Circle shares. A lower applicable VWAP would require more shares for a given dollar amount; a higher VWAP would require fewer. 
Binance Added 1.24 Million CRCL Shares at a Fixed Price
Circle issued Binance 1,237,011 Class A shares on Sept. 17 for $100 million at $80.84 each. Circle said the purchase price represented a 5% discount to CRCL’s market price before closing. The private placement closed around the same time as the companies entered into an expanded five-year commercial agreement. 
Because that transaction has closed, the Binance share count is fixed, and the shares have already been issued.
Binance also agreed to restrictions on selling, transferring, pledging, or hedging the shares until the earlier of the second anniversary of closing or certain termination events under the commercial agreement, subject to customary exceptions. Binance retains voting rights during that period.
Tazapay Could Require More Shares if CRCL’s Closing VWAP Is Lower
Circle’s agreement to acquire Tazapay uses a floating share-count structure.
The transaction carries a $400 million base purchase price, subject to adjustments including Tazapay debt, transaction expenses, and cash. Circle will pay the adjusted acquisition consideration in Class A common stock. Circle’s 8-K states that the aggregate consideration will consist of a number of Class A shares calculated using the adjusted purchase price and the Closing Stock Price. 
The agreement defines the “Closing Stock Price” as CRCL’s volume-weighted average closing price on the NYSE over the 20 consecutive trading days ending with the trading day immediately before closing. That price will determine how many Circle shares are required for the applicable dollar consideration.
At least five business days before closing, Tazapay must deliver an Estimated Closing Date Statement that produces the Estimated Purchase Price. No later than 90 days after closing, Circle’s acquisition subsidiary must deliver a Closing Date Statement calculating the Purchase Price, after which the agreement provides for a dispute process if the parties disagree with the calculation. 
Thursday’s CRCL price does not determine the acquisition share count. Circle expects the transaction to close in 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other closing conditions.
A $90.80 VWAP Would Require About 405,000 More Shares Than $100
The share-count sensitivity can be shown using illustrative prices.
If the adjusted Tazapay consideration were exactly $400 million and the applicable Closing Stock Price were $100, Circle would issue about 4.00 million shares.
At a hypothetical $90.80 Closing Stock Price, the same $400 million consideration would require approximately 4.405 million shares, or about 405,000 additional shares.
Those figures are illustrations only. The initial closing share count will depend on the applicable CRCL VWAP and the Estimated Purchase Price. The acquisition-related share count can then change after closing when the Purchase Price is finalized under the agreement’s true-up process. 
The agreement also provides for 5% and 3% indemnity holdbacks. Shares representing those amounts are to be placed in separate holdback reserves, and sellers will not have voting or economic rights in those shares until they are released. The holdbacks form part of the aggregate share consideration rather than additional purchase price.
Combined Equity Issuance Could Exceed 5 Million Shares in Illustrative Scenarios
As of July 30, Circle reported 234,685,190 Class A shares outstanding. Class B shares outstanding totaled 19,190,691. Together, the two classes represented 253,875,881 shares. This historical share count should not be used as a current fully diluted denominator. 
Binance’s 1.237 million newly issued shares equal approximately 0.49% of that July 30 share base.
If Circle were to issue 4.00 million shares for Tazapay at the illustrative $100 price, the Binance issuance and hypothetical Tazapay issuance would total about 5.24 million shares, representing roughly 2.06% of the July 30 share count.
At the illustrative $90.80 price, the combined amount would rise to about 5.64 million shares, or approximately 2.22% of that historical base.
Those percentages do not reflect dilution that has already occurred. Only the Binance shares have been issued. The Tazapay shares remain contingent on closing, and Circle’s outstanding share count may change before then through equity awards, option exercises, vesting, or other transactions.
Tazapay Deal Also Includes a $25 Million RSU Pool
The acquisition agreement provides for a separate $25 million restricted-stock-unit program for certain Tazapay employees selected by mutual agreement before closing.
Within 45 days after closing, Circle’s acquisition subsidiary must grant the awards, with the number of underlying shares determined using the same Closing Stock Price applied to the transaction consideration. 
At an illustrative $100 Closing Stock Price, $25 million would correspond to about 250,000 RSUs. At $90.80, it would correspond to approximately 275,000.
The RSUs are separate from the acquisition consideration and are not shares already outstanding. The awards vest in eight equal quarterly installments, with the first 12.5% installment scheduled for the standard quarterly vesting date closest to 27 months after the acquisition closes.
Final Tazapay Share Count Will Depend on CRCL’s Pre-Closing VWAP
Circle said Tazapay has more than $25 billion in annualized payment volume, more than 60 banking and fintech partners, and payout rails across more than 100 markets. The company said roughly 60% of Tazapay’s transaction volume involved stablecoins as of July 31.
Circle says the acquisition is intended to accelerate Circle Payments Network by adding Tazapay’s banking relationships, local payout rails and payments infrastructure across APAC and emerging markets. Circle has said the combination would expand its ability to originate and terminate cross-border payments and increase USDC distribution.
Binance’s equity issuance is already fixed at 1,237,011 shares. Tazapay’s share count, by contrast, will depend on the Estimated Purchase Price and CRCL’s 20-trading-day volume-weighted average closing price immediately before closing and may subsequently change through the agreement’s post-closing purchase-price true-up.

title: Circle of Life to acquire Washington Regional Hospice
content:
Circle of Life to acquire Washington Regional Hospice
LOWELL, Ark (KNWA/KFTA) — Circle of Life, an organization providing end-of-life care to hospice patients, is set to acquire the Washington Regional Hospice and purchase the Willard Walker Hospice Home in Fayetteville.
Washington Regional and Circle of Life announced the transition in an August press release, stating that the acquisition would allow the organizations to provide broader services, "ensuring every family has the support they need."
NWA Food Bank receives donation to kick off Walmart NW Arkansas Championship week
"We have made a commitment to the Northwest Arkansas community for years that we would be here to provide the exceptional care our team has always been known for. And we have grown right alongside that community. And so, any opportunity to provide more of that care and better care, we're going to take advantage of that opportunity," said Catherine Grubbs, chief executive officer of Circle of Life.
Circle of Life provides serious illness and end-of-life care to patients, as well as bereavement support for families. The organization has served Northwest Arkansans since 1992, and has recently expanded to serve northeast Oklahoma as well.
Grubbs, who has been a part of Circle of Life for about 16 years, stated that discussions with Washington Regional Health System about a potential transition began about three years ago.
"It was really a matter of no longer duplicating services," Grubbs said. "We're both non-profits serving our community, giving the best care possible, and we just started conversations. Our boards of directors were very supportive of this acquisition."
The Willard Walker Hospice Home would become Circle of Life's third hospice inpatient facility, in addition to its current facilities in Springdale and Bentonville.
Circle of Life will take on all home-based patients receiving care from Washington Regional Hospice, unless those patients choose to switch to another hospice provider.
"Even with growth, we are incredibly committed to maintaining the exceptional care that our organization is known for. We've added a number of team members, and we make sure that they are not only great caregivers, but they're a cultural fit in the organization because it's all about our people. And if we're taking good care of them, they can take good care of our community," Grubbs said.
The acquisition is set to close on Sept. 30. The Willard Walker Hospice Home will reopen as the Circle of Life Willard Walker Hospice Home early next year, but Washington Regional Hospice patients will receive uninterrupted care during the transition period.
"In hospice care, we have a saying that we get one chance to get it right," Grubbs said. "You don't get do-overs. And we take that really seriously. We stand in what we consider very sacred space with patients and families and try to have a very positive impact on that time that we have with them, which is often this last chapter of their life."

title: Binance Takes $100M Circle Stake in 5-Year USDC Deal
content:
Circle sold Binance 1.24M Class A shares at $80.84 each and will pay monthly fees tied to USDC held through its wallet infrastructure under a new 5-year pact.
Stablecoin News
Binance and Circle closed two separate but connected transactions on Sept. 17, combining an equity sale with a commercial agreement that sends money in both directions.
Circle sold 1,237,011 Class A common shares to Binance at $80.84 each through an unregistered private placement, raising $100 million in total. The price was set at a discount to Circle's market value before the transaction closed. Circle's stock trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker CRCL and closed at $94.29 on Sept. 21, rising more than 1.3% in premarket trading after the filing went public.
At that price, the value of Binance's holding stood at roughly $116.9 million. The exchange cannot convert any of that gain into cash while the lockup restrictions remain in force.
What Binance Agreed To
As part of the equity terms, Binance cannot sell, transfer, pledge, or hedge the shares for two years from the closing date. That restriction lifts earlier if Binance terminates the commercial arrangement under specific conditions. Standard carve-outs apply, including affiliate transfers, board-approved acquisitions, and disposals required by law. Binance keeps full voting rights on the shares throughout the lockup period.
Because the shares were sold through an unregistered placement, Binance's ability to resell them is limited unless the stock is registered or a legal exemption applies.
The Deal's History and Context
This is the third iteration of a Binance-Circle partnership in under two years. The new agreement replaces deals signed in November 2024 and August 2025. The first version was unveiled at Abu Dhabi Finance Week in December 2024, when Binance committed to making USDC available across its products and holding it in its corporate treasury.
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the investment reflects a long-term view on dollar access. "A stable, trusted digital dollar should not be a privilege, it should be available to anyone with a phone," Teng said in an emailed statement. Circle co-founder and CEO Jeremy Allaire said both companies see opportunities to use USDC to reach individuals and businesses across global emerging markets, particularly for savings and payments products.

title: Binance buys $100 million stake in Circle, expands partnership
content:
Binance buys $100 million stake in Circle, expands partnership

Circle shares were last up nearly 2 per cent in premarket trading.
Here are more details:

Circle issued Binance 1,237,011 Class A common shares at $80.84 apiece through a private placement that closed on Sept. 17, according to a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The SEC is a U.S. regulator overseeing publicly traded companies.

title: Binance bought a $100 million stake in Circle and signed a five-year deal to boost its stablecoin
content:
Circle Internet Group disclosed in a regulatory filing Tuesday that Binance purchased $100 million worth of Circle stock and entered into a new five-year agreement to promote USDC, the dollar-pegged stablecoin Circle issues.
The crypto exchange purchased roughly 1.24 million shares of Circle stock at a 5% discount and agreed to promote USDC on its platform
The stock sale and commercial agreement both closed on September 17, the filing said. Binance paid $80.84 per share for 1,237,011 shares of Circle's Class A common stock, a price the filing characterized as below the market rate at the time of closing. According to Unchained Crypto, that price was roughly 5% below Circle's September 17 closing price of $85.09.
Under the commercial arrangement, the filing said, Circle will pay Binance a monthly fee calculated as a portion of USDC balances held through its Modular Smart Contract Wallet infrastructure service, in exchange for Binance promoting USDC on its platform. Either party can terminate the agreement early under certain specified circumstances.
The new arrangement supersedes agreements the two companies reached in November 2024 and August 2025, the filing said. According to Unchained Crypto, the 2024 deal included a $60.25 million upfront payment to Binance plus monthly fees tied to its USDC balances and ran for two years; the new agreement runs for five.
The filing said Binance is prohibited from selling, pledging, or hedging its shares for a period of two years from closing, or until it exits the commercial deal under specified conditions, with standard carve-outs that cover affiliate transfers and legally mandated disposals. Binance's voting rights on those shares remain intact throughout the lock-up period.
"Our $100 million investment and five-year commitment represent long-duration conviction," Richard Teng, co-CEO of Binance, said in a statement. "A stable, trusted digital dollar should not be a privilege — it should be available to anyone with a phone."
"Together, we see incredible opportunities to leverage USDC to expand dollar access, support savings and investment with innovative digital asset products, and reach people and businesses throughout global emerging markets," Circle co-founder, chairman, and CEO Jeremy Allaire said in a statement.
Circle stock gained close to 2% in premarket trading Tuesday. USDC's total market cap stands at roughly $75 billion.

title: Binance Takes $100M Circle Stake in Strategic USDC Move
content:
Binance purchased $100 million of Circle Internet Group (NYSE: CRCL) shares on September 17, 2026, tying it to a five-year deal that pays it to promote USDC.
The Big Picture
- Binance bought 1.24 million Class A Circle shares at $80.84 each through a private placement that closed September 17.
- The price sat 14% below Circle’s prior closing price of $94.49, according to Yahoo Finance.
- Binance cannot sell, transfer or hedge the shares for up to two years but keeps voting rights.
- Circle will pay Binance a monthly incentive fee tied to USDC held through its Modular Smart Contract Wallet service.
- The deal replaces earlier USDC agreements the companies signed in November 2024 and August 2025.
Binance Locks In a Two-Year Hold
Circle issued Binance 1,237,011 Class A shares in a private placement, according to an SEC filing the company published. The filing states Binance agreed it “will not sell, transfer, assign, pledge, hypothecate or otherwise dispose of” the shares until the earlier of two years from closing or a termination of the commercial arrangements by Binance under specified conditions, subject to customary exceptions for affiliate transfers.
Binance keeps the right to vote the shares throughout the lockup. The unregistered placement also blocks resale unless the shares are later registered or an exemption applies.
Circle’s Class A stock closed Monday at $94.49, up 2.95% on the day, before trading near $95.76 in Tuesday premarket action, according to Yahoo Finance. Circle’s market capitalization stood near $25.8 billion at the time of the deal.
BREAKING: @Binance buys $100M in @Circle shares as part of a five-year $USDC promotion deal, receiving 1.24M Class A shares at $80.84 each in a private placement with a two-year lock-up on the stake. pic.twitter.com/LjALWoKbY9
— CoinDesk (@CoinDesk) September 22, 2026
A Wider USDC Promotion Deal
The share purchase closed alongside an expanded version of the companies’ existing USDC partnership. Circle agreed to calculate a monthly incentive fee as a percentage of USDC balances held through its Modular Smart Contract Wallet and pay that fee to Binance. In return, Binance will run promotional activities for USDC across its platform for five years.
The arrangement supersedes agreements signed in November 2024 and August 2025. Either party can end the five-year partnership early if specified events occur, though the exact triggers are not public. Circle’s subsidiaries, rather than the parent company, signed the commercial agreements.
USDC currently ranks as the sixth largest crypto asset by market value, at roughly $74.6 billion, per Yahoo Finance market data. The stablecoin already trades on Binance under the original tie-up, announced in December 2024 when Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire and Binance CEO Richard Teng unveiled a strategic partnership at Abu Dhabi Finance Week. Circle has also kept expanding USDC’s reach across other chains.
Competing Exchange Stablecoin Deals
Exchanges routinely pay for stablecoin placement, a dynamic visible across broader crypto exchange trading volume, but Circle’s move to pair equity with a revenue-linked fee stands out.
- Coinbase holds an equity stake in Circle and splits USDC reserve revenue with the issuer under a long running partnership.
- Kraken has built out stablecoin-linked payment tools, including deposit features connecting multiple exchanges.
- OKX continues expanding USDT and USDC trading pairs across its app-based markets.
- KuCoin sells bulk USDT and USDC gift cards aimed at retail stablecoin demand.
- Tether, USDC’s chief rival, reported strong second-quarter 2026 profit alongside continued USDT supply growth.
The Bottom Line
The deal turns Binance from a stablecoin distribution partner into a Circle shareholder with a direct financial stake in USDC’s growth. A monthly incentive fee tied to wallet balances gives Binance a recurring reason to keep pushing USDC volume rather than treating the stablecoin as one option among several on its platform.
The two-year lockup limits how quickly Binance can exit the position, signaling the arrangement is meant to outlast a single market cycle. Pricing the placement 14% below market value suggests Circle weighed the promotional reach and fee structure as worth more than a full-price share sale, a trade other stablecoin issuers may watch as they negotiate their own exchange partnerships.

Binance Takes $100M Stake in Circle Under Five-Year USDC Promotion Deal
decrypt.co

In brief
Circle issued Binance 1,237,011 Class A shares at $80.84 each, raising $100 million in a private placement that closed September 17.
Under a separate five-year deal, Circle will pay Binance a monthly fee set as a percentage of the $USDC held through its wallet infrastructure.
Binance cannot sell or hedge the stock for up to two years but keeps its voting rights.
Stablecoin issuer Circle sold Binance 1,237,011 Class A shares at $80.84 apiece, raising $100 million in a private placement that closed on September 17, according to an 8-K filed Tuesday.
The placement closed immediately after an expanded commercial deal running the other way. Circle agreed to pay Binance a monthly incentive fee set as a percentage of the $USDC held through its Modular Smart Contract Wallet infrastructure service, and Binance agreed to promote the stablecoin on its platform. The arrangement runs five years, and either side can terminate early if specified events occur.

It is the third version of the tie-up in under two years. The filing says it supersedes and replaces agreements the two entered in November 2024 and August 2025. The first was unveiled at Abu Dhabi Finance Week that December, when Binance said it would make $USDC available across its products and hold the stablecoin in its corporate treasury.
Binance has agreed not to sell, transfer, pledge or hedge the shares for two years from closing, or until it terminates the commercial arrangements in certain circumstances, whichever comes first. Affiliate transfers, a board-approved takeover and disposals required by law are excepted. It keeps every shareholder right in the meantime, including the vote.
The stock went at a discount to Circle's market price before closing, though the filing does not say how large. CRCL was trading in the mid-$80s on September 17, then rose through the following sessions to close at $94.49 on September 21. At that price Binance's 1,237,011 shares are worth around $116.9 million, some $16.9 million more than it paid, none of which it can realise. The stock is still down about 34% over 12 months, against a 16.5% gain for the S&P 500.
The deal closed a day after Circle switched on Arc, a Layer 1 network with BlackRock, DTCC and Visa among its founding validators and $USDC as its gas token. Binance is one of the exchanges providing routes onto it.
Paying for distribution is how $USDC has always reached users. Coinbase, which co-founded the stablecoin, has taken half the interest earned on its reserves. Compass Point analysts began coverage of Circle at neutral in June 2025, reasoning that its distribution partners were confined largely to crypto firms. The Binance fee adds a second exchange to the payroll, this one holding stock in the issuer paying it.
The filing landed a day after Bloomberg reported that federal prosecutors are investigating whether Binance breached U.S. sanctions on Iran.

title: citybiz+Circle Pharma Secures $92.5M Series E Funding to Advance Cancer Therapy
content:
Circle Pharma, a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing cancer therapies, has announced the closing of an oversubscribed $92.5 million Series E financing led by The Column Group. Other existing and new investors included Boston’s Nextech Invest and RA Capital Management, New York-based Euclidean Capital, and Eli Lilly and Co. Circle Pharma, based in South San Francisco, has raised a total of approximately $302.5 million to date.
The company was founded in 2012 by Matthew P. Jacobson, professor and chair of Pharmaceutical Chemistry at UC San Francisco, and R. Scott Lokey, professor of Chemistry and Biochemistry at UC Santa Cruz. It focuses on macrocycles — large, ring-shaped molecular structures typically containing 12 or more atoms that bridge the gap between traditional small-molecule drugs and large biological therapies like antibodies. Macrocycles combine the high target selectivity and potency of biologics with the metabolic benefits and potential for oral delivery found in small molecules.
The company said it would use the proceeds of the funding round to advance CID-165, a first-in-class oral macrocyclic cyclin D1 RxL inhibitor, through early clinical development for estrogen receptor-positive (ER-positive) breast cancer and the continued development of Circle Pharma’s broader pipeline of cyclin-targeted macrocycles.
“We believe CID-165 has the potential to become a new backbone therapy for ER-positive breast cancer and this financing provides us with the resources to generate meaningful clinical data to validate that potential,” said Circle Pharma President and CEO David J. Earp, J.D., Ph.D. “Progress across our pipeline underscores the ability of our platform to generate first-in-class compounds across the previously undrugged family of cyclins, the master regulators of the cell cycle.”
Earp previously held senior positions in Geron Corp., where he led the spin-out of Geron’s nuclear transfer technology into StART Licensing and its subsequent acquisition by Viagen Corp. He holds a PhD. in Biochemistry and Molecular Biology from the University of Cambridge, and a J.D. (magna cum laude) from the Northwestern School of Law of Lewis and Clark College.

For broader crypto context, the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (NASDAQ:IBIT) is down 3% to $43.26. Circle Internet stock is still up 25% over the past month, so today’s decline gives back part of a run rather than breaking new ground.

ARK Invest also pared nearly every other crypto-linked position it holds, including its Coinbase and Bitmine stakes.
The concentration is what separates Circle Internet from the rest of the group today. Circle Internet is falling roughly half again as hard as Coinbase and Bitmine, and the ARK Invest trim is the piece the others don’t carry. The same manager cut all three names, but the heaviest hand landed on Circle Internet.
Clarity Act Vote Cuts Both Ways
The Senate is holding a procedural vote today on the Clarity Act, and the pending framework cuts both ways for Circle Internet. Legislation that legitimizes stablecoins also clears a path for bank-issued competitors with cheaper funding and established customer bases. That’s why Circle Internet is trading heavier than peers even before the outcome is known.
The bull case for Circle Internet argues that regulatory clarity is worth more to a regulated stablecoin issuer than to anyone else in the complex. The bear case flags that today’s vote is procedural rather than final, so the uncertainty around Circle Internet doesn’t end whichever way the count lands. Coinbase and Bitmine face the same overhang without the same idiosyncratic supply pressure from a high-profile institutional seller.
What to Watch Next
Circle Internet’s near-term direction hinges on the vote’s outcome and on whether ARK Invest disclosures later this week extend the trim. Investors can watch for signs that Coinbase and Bitmine stabilize first if the Clarity Act clears its procedural hurdle, since Circle Internet has more overhang left to work through. title: Why Circle Internet Group Slumped by 11% This Week
content:
Circle Internet Group (CRCL +0.48%) had a week to forget, as far as its equity was concerned. After the cryptocurrency developer announced an acquisition on Tuesday, many investors bailed from its stock. Ultimately, Circle shrank by 11% over the Labor Day-shortened trading week, according to data compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence.
Paying for Tazapay
Before market open Tuesday, Circle divulged that it had signed a definitive agreement to acquire Singapore-based Tazapay. The Asian company specializes in cross-border business-to-business (B2B) payment technology.
Speaking of payments, Circle has agreed to hand over $400 million in newly issued common stock to purchase its asset-to-be.
In the press release trumpeting the deal, Circle said that the take-up and acceptance of USDC, the prominent stablecoin it developed, will be enhanced by its ownership of Tazapay.
It quoted its co-founder and CEO, Jeremy Allaire, as saying that "stablecoin settlement is becoming core infrastructure in the global economy, and combining USDC with Tazapay's world-class banking relationships, local payout rails, and institutional customer base will accelerate worldwide USDC adoption."
NYSE: CRCL
Key Data Points
400 million reasons for skepticism
I'd say that's accurate, assuming Circle can effectively integrate Tazapay with its business. However, there was clear skepticism about the deal from both investors and analysts tracking Circle's stock. One of the latter, Mizuho's Dan Dolev, felt compelled to publish an update reiterating his underperform (read: sell) recommendation and $45-per-share price target.
According to reports, Dolev doubts that owning Tazapay will make much of a difference to Circle's performance, and the Singapore company's volume and reach aren't considerable. It also doesn't solve the increasing problem of competition, as in his view, stablecoins are rapidly becoming commoditized.

title: Circle to buy Tazapay for $400m, a year after joining its cap table
content:
NYSE-listed US stablecoin issuer Circle Internet Group has agreed to acquire Singapore-based cross-border payments firm Tazapay in an all-stock transaction carrying aggregate consideration of $400 million—twice the valuation the company commanded in a Series B financing earlier this year, according to DealStreetAsia DATA VANTAGE.
The acquisition also comes just over a year after Circle entered Tazapay’s cap table.
The purchase price was not disclosed in Circle’s announcement of the deal, but was detailed in a regulatory filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission.
The transaction set up an exit for a group of investors including top shareholder Peak XV Partners, Ripple, Coinbase Ventures and CMT Digital.
Top shareholders of Tazapay
Under the agreement, a wholly-owned Circle subsidiary will acquire all outstanding shares in Tazapay that are not already held by Circle or its affiliates. The sellers will receive Circle Class A common shares equivalent to $400 million, subject to adjustments for Tazapay’s cash, outstanding debt and transaction expenses.
“Stablecoin settlement is becoming core infrastructure in the global economy, and combining USDC with Tazapay’s world-class banking relationships, local payout rails, and institutional customer base will accelerate worldwide USDC adoption,” said Jeremy Allaire, Co-Founder, CEO, and Chairman at Circle.
Circle’s most recent acquisitions before Tazapay include Taiwan-based crypto infrastructure provider CYBAVO and payments orchestration startup Elements, both acquired in 2022.
Under the all-stock deal, Tazapay shareholders will receive shares in NYSE-listed Circle in exchange for their holdings in the privately held Singapore company, rather than cash consideration.
The transaction is expected to close in 2027, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals, including from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).
The deal comes barely six months after Circle Ventures led an extension of Tazapay’s Series B round in March, bringing the total size of the financing to $36 million. Coinbase Ventures and CMT Digital joined as new investors in the extension, alongside Peak XV, GMO Venture Partners and January Capital. Ripple, Norinchukin Capital, ARC180 and RTP Global were also existing backers.
Circle had joined Tazapay’s cap table in a Series B tranche in August 2025, alongside Peak XV, Ripple, Norinchukin Capital and GMO VenturePartners. January Capital, ARC180 and RTP Global also participated in that round.
“This acquisition will increase Circle’s capability to originate and terminate payments globally, near-instant and 24/7, which is a meaningful step toward making USDC the default payment rail for cross-border commerce,” said Irfan Ganchi, Senior Vice President of Payments at Circle.
Circle said the acquisition will accelerate the global expansion of its payments infrastructure. Tazapay processes more than $25 billion in annualised payment volume and has local payout rails across more than 100 markets. About 60% of its transaction volume already involves stablecoins, according to a statement.
The acquisition comes as stablecoins move deeper into mainstream payments infrastructure, particularly in cross-border transactions. Stablecoins processed $33 trillion in transaction volume in 2025, up 72% from a year earlier, while investors have increasingly shifted capital toward the licensed payment rails, banking partnerships and cross-border networks that enable their use.
Southeast Asia has emerged as a key testing ground for that shift, given its fragmented payments landscape and high volume of cross-border commerce.
Circle follows a recent string of deals and funding activity around stablecoin payments infrastructure in Asia. Kraken acquired Hong Kong-based stablecoin payments firm Reap Technologies for up to $600 million, while KAST and Fasset have raised fresh capital to expand stablecoin-powered payments and banking infrastructure across the region.

title: Circle to Acquire Singapore's Tazapay for $400 Million in Stock – Its Largest Deal Since Poloniex

Tazapay operates a payment gateway spanning more than 173 countries, global collection accounts in over 35 currencies and payout capability in more than 80 markets, built on relationships with over 60 banking and fintech partners. The company serves more than 1,000 businesses across 30 countries and holds payment licenses in Singapore, Canada, Australia and the United States, with applications pending in the European Union, Hong Kong and the United Arab Emirates. It has doubled revenue in each of the past three years and closed a Series B extension round led by Circle Ventures in March 2026. Tazapay and Circle have collaborated on Circle's Payments Network since 2025.

Circle said the deal gives it regulated banking connections across more than 100 markets without having to build country-by-country payment networks itself, and that it does not expect any disruption to Tazapay's existing customers, APIs or pricing once the acquisition closes.

title: Circle agrees to buy cross-border payments firm Tazapay for $400 million
content:
Circle agrees to buy cross-border payments firm Tazapay for $400 million
The deal could grant Circle vital, regulated "last-mile" infrastructure, bridging the gap between stablecoins and traditional local banking systems.
- Circle agreed to acquire Tazapay for $400 million in stock, in its largest acquisition since that of crypto exchange Poloniex in 2018.
- Tazapay processes over $25 billion in annual volume across 100 markets, with roughly 60% of transaction volume already involving stablecoins.
Stablecoin issuer Circle agreed to pay $400 million in stock for Singapore-based cross-border payments company Tazapay in one of its largest publicly disclosed acquisitions to date.
The USDC issuer will calculate the number of shares using their volume-weighted average closing price during the 20 trading days before the deal closes, according to a regulatory filing. The price will be adjusted for Tazapay’s debt, transaction expenses and cash.
Tazapay is a business-to-business payments infrastructure firm that connects payment companies and financial institutions to more than 60 banking and fintech partners, allowing them to collect and pay out money through local rails in over 100 markets, according to its website.
The company processes more than $25 billion in annualized payment volume, with approximately 60% of transactions already involving stablecoins, Circle said.
Tazapay said in March that it served more than 1,000 companies and fintech firms across 30 countries and had doubled revenue for three consecutive years. That came alongside a Series B funding round extension led by Circle Ventures.
The firm holds licenses or registrations in Singapore, Canada, Australia and the U.S., with applications underway in the European Union, Hong Kong and the United Arab Emirates.
Stablecoins can move across blockchains globally, but turning them into local currency still requires regulated intermediary companies, bank accounts and payout connections in individual markets. Tazapay would give Circle much of that last-mile infrastructure instead of requiring it to build the network country by country.
Circle was already familiar with the business. Tazapay has helped design Circle Payments Network since 2025, according to Circle’s acquisition announcement.
The purchase continues a series of acquisitions from Circle. It paid approximately $100 million for Hashnote, the company behind tokenized money-market fund USYC, in 2025. It bought web3 infrastructure provider Cybavo in 2022. The acquistion of Tazapay is Circle’s most expensive since its 2018 purchase of crypto exchange Poloniex.
Circle also paid $209.9 million in stock for Coinbase’s remaining half of the Centre Consortium, which controlled USDC’s intellectual property, in 2023.
It has separately acquired payments software company Elements, blockchain consensus technology Malachite and, in July, nearly 1,000 blockchain patents from IBM.
The Tazapay acquisition is expected to close in 2027 and requires regulatory approvals, including from the Monetary Authority of Singapore. Tazapay’s services, pricing and support are expected to remain unchanged while the transaction is pending.

Now, Circle is moving from investor and partner to owner.
For Tazapay’s customers, Circle said there will be no immediate changes to its products, APIs, pricing or support when the transaction closes.

Small business lender Funding Circle has revealed plans for its boss of more than four years to step down by next September as it upped its annual profit outlook.
The group said Lisa Jacobs is set to leave “no later” than September 2027 and will now kick off the search for her replacement.
Ms Jacobs has been with the group since 2012 and was appointed chief executive in January 2022.

It hiked its full-year outlook to more than £40 million in pre-tax profits and £255 million in revenues following the strong first half, up from previous guidance for profits of at least £35 million and revenues of around £235 million.
But shares in the FTSE 250 listed firm fell 11% in Tuesday morning trading despite the profit cheer.
Outgoing boss Ms Jacobs said the results show the business is “in the best position that it has ever been”.
She said: “We have shown strong growth and profitability and great foundations for the future – and now feels like the right time to start the process of handing over the reins.”
The group’s chairman, Ken Stannard, paid tribute to Lisa’s “outstanding and ongoing contribution to Funding Circle”.
“She has transformed the business, advanced our mission and built a great team,” he said.
“When she joined in 2012, Funding Circle was a start-up built on a simple conviction: that technology could transform how small businesses access finance.
“Since then, we’ve extended more than £18 billion in credit to more than 135,000 SMEs, and delivered the transformation plan set out in March 2024 to build a simpler, high-growth and more profitable business.”
Ms Jacobs took on the top job when former chief executive and co-founder Samir Desai stepped aside.
Funding Circle was set up in August 2010 by three university friends – Mr Desai, James Meekings and Andrew Mullinger.

title: Circle to Acquire Singapore's Tazapay, Expanding USDC Cross-Border Payment Network
content:
Circle to Acquire Singapore's Tazapay, Expanding USDC Cross-Border Payment Network
Circle, the issuer of the USDC stablecoin, announced on the 8th that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Tazapay, a Singapore-based cross-border payments infrastructure company. The transaction is targeted to close in 2027, subject to approval from the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and other customary closing conditions.
The acquisition will significantly expand Circle's payment corridors across Asia-Pacific and emerging markets. Tazapay processes more than $25 billion in annualized payment volume and maintains over 60 banking and fintech partners with access to more than 100 markets. Stablecoins are utilized in approximately 60% of all transactions.
Irfan Ganchi, Circle's Senior Vice President of Payments, said, "This acquisition will strengthen Circle's ability to initiate and settle payments globally. Near-instant, 24/7 settlement represents meaningful progress toward making USDC the default payment method for cross-border commerce."
Tazapay has served as a design partner for the Circle Payments Network (CPN) since 2025. Circle emphasized that existing Tazapay customers will see no changes to their current services, APIs, pricing, or support structures following the acquisition.
The two companies share a deep history. Circle previously invested in Tazapay and participated in the company's Series B round in August 2025. Ripple, the issuer of XRP, also joined as an investor in that round. According to data from market research firm Traxcn, Tazapay's cumulative funding reached $57.9 million at that time.
Tazapay's growth trajectory has been steep. Its annualized payment volume stood at $10 billion as of August 2025, and has since grown 2.5x to $25 billion in just over a year. With stablecoins accounting for 60% of transaction volume, Circle stands to benefit from both securing real-world use cases for USDC and integrating payment network infrastructure.
Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. Circle's stock, listed on the New York Stock Exchange, fell more than 2% in pre-market trading on the day, according to Yahoo Finance.
As the stablecoin market experiences rapid growth, Circle is pursuing a strategy of directly acquiring payment infrastructure to drive real-world USDC adoption. Once the acquisition is completed, Circle will hold not only its stablecoin issuance business but also the actual payment pipelines through which transactions flow, further strengthening its position in the cross-border payments market.

title: Circle Seals Tazapay Deal to Widen USDC Payment Rails
content:
Circle Internet Group (NYSE: CRCL) signed a definitive agreement on September 8, 2026 to buy Tazapay, a Singapore-based B2B payments platform where stablecoins already move about 60% of transaction volume. The deal is expected to close in 2027.
The Big Picture
- Circle agreed to acquire Tazapay, a Singapore cross-border payments company serving payment service providers and financial institutions.
- Tazapay handles more than $25 billion in annualized payment volume across local payout rails in over 100 markets.
- Stablecoins already sit inside roughly 60% of Tazapay’s transaction volume, a share Circle disclosed in the announcement.
- The Monetary Authority of Singapore must approve the transaction before it can close, alongside customary conditions.
- Tazapay customers keep their existing service, APIs, pricing and support, Circle said, with no disruption planned.
Circle buys local rails into 100 payout markets
Circle said the agreement brings 60+ banking and fintech partners and local payout coverage in more than 100 markets into its ecosystem. Tazapay has worked as a design partner for Circle Payments Network since 2025, so the two firms have already built against each other’s systems.
The customer base is the asset. Tazapay sells to payment service providers and financial institutions, so every client on its book carries its own downstream volume. Circle is buying wholesale distribution for USDC, one layer above the merchants who eventually touch the money.
Circle has signed an agreement to acquire @tazapay, a cross-border payments company supporting businesses across 100+ markets.
Tazapay brings a payments-native team, 60+ banking and fintech partners, and meaningful stablecoin payment volume, with more than 60% of its volume…
The 60% stablecoin share is the number that matters
The $25 billion annualized volume figure will draw the attention. The share already touching stablecoins is the more useful number. Roughly 60% of Tazapay transactions include them today, which means most of the conversion work inside these flows has already happened, and Circle inherits demand it would otherwise have to build.
The rest of that volume still runs on conventional banking rails, and Circle has not said what happens to it after close.
Implications for cross-border settlement
Irfan Ganchi, Circle’s senior vice president of payments, said the acquisition will increase the company’s capability to “originate and terminate payments globally, near-instant and 24/7, which is a meaningful step toward making USDC the default payment rail for cross-border commerce.“
Controlling both ends of a payment strips out the correspondent banking hops that set settlement times in emerging markets. Card networks have chased the same effect by attaching stablecoin payouts to rails they already own, as Visa did in its stablecoin payouts deal with Zero Hash.
Four questions stay open. What is Circle paying? What conditions will MAS attach? Does Tazapay keep its brand? How is the non-stablecoin portion of its volume treated? The announcement answers none of them.
Tazapay customers have nothing to change today. Circle said service, APIs, pricing and support continue as they are. Businesses routing payouts through the platform can treat MAS clearance and the 2027 close as the checkpoints where settlement terms and contracts could be revisited.
The Bottom Line
This acquisition reads as a distribution purchase rather than a technology one. Circle already holds the stablecoin, the network and the regulatory standing. What it lacked was licensed local payout capacity in the emerging markets where cross-border demand is growing fastest, and Tazapay supplies that across more than 100 markets with the bank relationships that make payouts land.
The cost of that capacity stays undisclosed, and a 2027 close gives competitors a long runway. Rahul Shinghal, Tazapay’s co-founder and chief executive, framed the sale around Circle’s dollar infrastructure and regulatory standing, the harder half of that pair to replicate. Stablecoin settlement volume concentrates where a licensed issuer meets working local rails, and this transaction puts both under one owner across Asia-Pacific, subject to the Singapore regulator signing off.

Circle to acquire Tazapay to expand USDC cross-border payments

Circle has agreed to acquire Singapore-based cross-border payments platform Tazapay in a $400 million all-stock deal expected to close in 2027.

The transaction will also require customary closing conditions and approval from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, Circle said in a Tuesday announcement.
Tazapay has more than $25 billion in annualized payment volume and serves more than 60 banking and fintech partners with local payout rails covering more than 100 markets. The company said in August 2025 that annualized payment volume was more than $10 billion.
Circle previously invested in Tazapay through Circle Ventures, including in the startup’s August 2025 Series B round. Tazapay has raised $57.9 million across five funding rounds, according to Tracxn data.
Stablecoins account for about 60% of Tazapay’s transaction volume, according to Circle. The company said the acquisition will expand its ability to route payments to and from Asia-Pacific and emerging markets.
“This acquisition will increase Circle’s capability to originate and terminate payments globally, near-instant and 24/7, which is a meaningful step toward making USDC the default payment rail for cross-border commerce,” said Irfan Ganchi, senior vice president of payments at Circle.
Tazapay has been a design partner for the Circle Payments Network since 2025. Circle said Tazapay customers should see no disruption to their services, APIs, pricing or support.

title: Funding Circle Lifts 2026 Profit Guide Above £40 Million; New Floor Allows a 34% H2 Drop
content:
Funding Circle has raised its 2026 revenue target to more than £255 million and its pre-tax-profit target to more than £40 million, but the new floor still carries a meaningful second-half cushion. After £24.1 million of profit before tax in the first six months, the lender could clear the full-year minimum with £15.9 million in the second half—a 34% sequential decline.
That arithmetic is the most useful way to read Tuesday’s upgrade. The headline is strong: Funding Circle’s previous targets were about £235 million of revenue and at least £35 million of pre-tax profit. Yet management has not annualized a first half in which revenue increased 50% to £138.2 million and pre-tax profit quadrupled from £6.0 million.
The September 8 regulatory results also add another share buyback of up to £25 million once the current program finishes. Separately, Funding Circle said chief executive Lisa Jacobs intends to step down by September 2027, giving the board a long search window but placing succession over the next phase of the growth plan.
The upgraded floor still permits a softer second half
Subtract the first-half result from the new full-year guidance and the implied minimum for July through December is £116.8 million of revenue and £15.9 million of pre-tax profit. Those figures would be 15.5% and 34.0% below the first half, respectively. The implied second-half margin at the minimum is about 13.6%, versus 17.4% in the first half.
A floor is not a forecast, and “more than” leaves room for a much better outcome. Still, the gap tells investors what management has protected against: borrower demand normalized in the second quarter after a particularly strong start to the year, while the newer FlexiPay and credit-card products require marketing spend and upfront recognition of expected credit losses.
The revenue threshold has more headroom than it first appears. Funding Circle generated £138.2 million in the first half, so merely repeating that performance would produce £276.4 million for the year—£21.4 million above the new minimum. The company also said it is trending toward the upper end of its £300 million to £350 million 2029 revenue range, assuming a stable economy.
Term Loans fund the experiment
The mature Term Loans unit remains the earnings engine. Originations rose 43% to £1.05 billion, revenue grew to £108.2 million, and pre-tax profit reached £28.6 million from £12.7 million. Its 26.4% pre-tax margin more than funded the £4.5 million loss in FlexiPay and credit cards.
Funding Circle has also moved its shorter-term loan product off its balance sheet and into its institutional platform model. That sale generated a £31.5 million net cash receipt after £105.7 million of associated borrowing was transferred to the buyer. Future originations under that arrangement earn transaction and servicing fees rather than requiring Funding Circle to hold the loans.
This matters because it preserves capital for FlexiPay. Unrestricted cash rose to £136.5 million from £100.9 million at year-end, and committed forward-flow funding for Term Loans stands at £2.4 billion. The platform model lets outside institutions take the underlying credit risk on those loans while Funding Circle earns fees.
FlexiPay’s growth and credit risk are moving together
FlexiPay and card transactions increased 71% to £640 million, while the segment’s revenue rose 83% to £30.0 million. Drawn balances reached £300 million, up from £169 million a year earlier, and active customers increased 48% to about 25,000. The segment’s loss narrowed from £6.7 million to £4.5 million.
The counterweight is the expected-credit-loss charge, which increased 81% to £15.2 million. That growth broadly matched the revenue expansion, and Funding Circle said credit performance remained in line with its expectations. But FlexiPay has less historical data than the mature loan book, making its impairment model one of the result’s most sensitive assumptions.
The allowance against drawn and undrawn FlexiPay credit lines was £47.2 million at June 30, based on a blended 9.2% probability of default for stage-one and stage-two exposures and an estimated 87.4% loss given default. Those are accounting estimates rather than predictions of realized loss. They become more consequential as the drawn book and £630.7 million of undrawn commitments expand.
What 230 pence prices in
The London Stock Exchange’s delayed quote page showed a September 7 reference close of 230 pence, a market value of £685.9 million and a 52-week high of 252.03 pence. At that reference price, Funding Circle was 8.7% below the high and valued at about 17.1 times the new minimum pre-tax profit.
The additional £25 million buyback is equivalent to roughly 3.6% of that market value, although the actual percentage retired will depend on the execution price. Funding Circle has bought about £72 million of shares since its repurchases began in 2024, representing roughly 18% of the issued share capital, and says the latest authorization will bring the announced total to £100 million.
The buyback supports per-share growth, but it does not settle the central debate. The stock needs Term Loans to keep supplying high-margin, capital-light earnings while FlexiPay scales toward profitability without an adverse turn in SME credit. The second-half revenue and profit cushion makes a guidance miss less likely; it also means investors should demand more than merely reaching the floor.
Succession adds a longer-dated execution test
Jacobs joined Funding Circle in 2012 and became CEO in January 2022. The separate succession announcement says she will remain in the role while the board searches for a replacement and will leave no later than September 2027.
That timetable reduces immediate disruption, but the next chief executive will inherit a business at an inflection point: the core platform is profitable, the newer revolving-credit products are growing quickly, and capital is being returned aggressively. For shareholders, the next proof points are second-half loan demand, FlexiPay loss rates, the segment’s path to profit and whether Funding Circle beats a guidance floor that its first-half numbers have already made conservative.

title: Yahoo Finance

Funding Circle (LSE:FCH) reported first-half 2026 revenue of £138.2 million, an increase of 50% year-on-year, as lending activity increased across its term loan, FlexiPay and credit card products.
Profit before tax rose to £24.1 million, approximately four times the prior-year level, while total credit extended increased 52% to £1.69 billion.
Assets under management reached £3.25 billion during the period.
Term Loan Originations Rise 43%
Funding Circle's term loan originations increased 43% to £1.05 billion in the first half.
The division generated profit before tax of £28.6 million and a PBT margin of 26.4%.
Activity across FlexiPay and credit cards also increased, with transaction volumes rising 71% to £640 million. Funding Circle said these businesses moved closer to breakeven during the period.
The company expanded funding capacity for these products through an increased facility with Citi.
Funding Circle Raises 2026 Guidance
Following its first-half performance, Funding Circle increased its financial guidance for 2026.
The company now expects full-year revenue of more than £255 million and profit before tax of more than £40 million.
Funding Circle also announced plans for an additional share buyback of up to £25 million. The programme would take total share repurchases since March 2024 to £100 million.
The company reported £2.4 billion of committed forward-flow funding arrangements and renewed funding lines to support future lending activity.
Funding Circle Targets £300 Million to £350 Million Revenue by 2029
Funding Circle uses proprietary data and artificial intelligence-based models in its credit assessment processes. Management said its AI-powered credit models outperform traditional credit scores.
The group continues to focus on expanding its products and reaching additional small and medium-sized businesses.
Funding Circle's medium-term targets include revenue of £300 million to £350 million by 2029 and a profit-before-tax margin in the low-to-mid-20% range.
These figures remain management targets and are not established future results.
More about Funding Circle Holdings plc
Funding Circle Holdings plc is a UK-based financial technology company providing financing products to small and medium-sized enterprises.
Its products include term loans, FlexiPay and credit cards. The company's platform uses proprietary data and automated credit-decision technology, with lending funded largely through institutional capital.
Funding Circle's business model is focused on providing multiple financing products to SMEs while using external funding arrangements to support lending activity.

title: Circle Agrees to Acquire Singapore Payments Firm Tazapay
content:
Digital Assets
Circle Agrees to Acquire Singapore Payments Firm Tazapay
Add Securities.io to your preferred sources on Google
Circle Internet Group, Inc. (CRCL ) said on September 8, 2026, that it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Tazapay, a Singapore-headquartered B2B cross-border payments infrastructure company focused on serving payment service providers and financial institutions. Circle said in an announcement that the transaction is expected to close in 2027, subject to customary closing conditions and receipt of regulatory approvals, including approval from the Monetary Authority of Singapore.
Tazapay brings more than $25 billion of annualized payment volume, more than 60 banking and fintech partners, and local payout rails covering over 100 markets, according to Circle. Approximately 60% of Tazapay’s transaction volume already includes stablecoins, the company said. Circle, the issuer of USDC, said the acquisition will accelerate its mission to build the infrastructure layer for global digital finance.
“Stablecoin settlement is becoming core infrastructure in the global economy and combining USDC with Tazapay’s world-class banking relationships, local payout rails, and institutional customer base will accelerate worldwide USDC adoption,” said Jeremy Allaire, co-founder, CEO, and chairman of Circle. Allaire said Tazapay has been a design partner for Circle Payments Network since 2025.
Irfan Ganchi, senior vice president of payments at Circle, said Tazapay brings deep payment infrastructure across APAC and emerging markets, where Circle sees increasing demand for USDC-denominated transactions. He said the acquisition will increase Circle’s capability to originate and terminate payments globally, near-instant and 24/7, and that, combined with Circle’s existing network, Tazapay extends coverage to move money anywhere stablecoin payments are being adopted globally.
“We built Tazapay to make payments faster, remove friction, and streamline dependency on banking rails that don’t operate at the speed of global commerce,” said Rahul Shinghal, co-founder and CEO of Tazapay. “Circle has the dollar infrastructure in USDC and the regulatory standing to take what we’ve built further than we could alone.”
Circle said Tazapay customers can expect no disruption to their service, APIs, pricing, or support. In a separate statement, Tazapay said customer contracts will continue on existing terms and that virtual accounts, payout routes, and settlement arrangements will continue as they are. The company said it will operate under the same brand, product, and roadmap, with the same team and the same licences, and that customers will hear directly from Tazapay before anything changes in the future.
An Existing Partnership
The agreement extends a relationship between the two companies that predates the acquisition. Circle announced Circle Payments Network on April 21, 2025, describing a network to connect banks, neo-banks, payment service providers, virtual asset service providers, and digital wallets and to enable real-time settlement of cross-border payments using regulated stablecoins. Tazapay was among the design partners Circle named at launch. The 2025 announcement said Banco Santander, Deutsche Bank, Société Générale, and Standard Chartered Bank contributed expertise to the network’s design, and that participants must meet eligibility standards covering licensing, AML/CFT compliance, financial risk management, and cybersecurity protocols.
In March 2026, Circle Ventures led an extension of Tazapay’s Series B round. Tazapay’s March 26, 2026 announcement said the extension brought total Series B funding to $36 million, with CMT Digital and Coinbase Ventures joining as new investors and Peak XV Partners, GMO Venture Partners, and January Capital participating. Tazapay said the capital would be deployed toward licensing expansion, go-to-market acceleration across Asia, Latin America, the Middle East, and the Americas, and the development of agentic payment infrastructure supporting autonomous, AI-driven payment flows on licensed infrastructure. The company described its offering at the time as regulated last-mile infrastructure using digital settlement technology for cross-border payments across emerging markets. In its statement on the acquisition, Tazapay said Circle had been a partner from the beginning of its stablecoin work before leading the Series B extension.
At the time of the extension, Tazapay said it served more than 1,000 enterprises and fintechs across 30 countries, with local collections and payouts in more than 70 markets. The company said it held licences and registrations in Singapore, Canada, Australia, and the United States, with active applications in the UAE, the EU, and Hong Kong.
Licensing History
Tazapay holds a Major Payment Institution licence from the Monetary Authority of Singapore. In an August 2, 2023 announcement of the licence, the company said it allows Tazapay to extend account issuance, merchant acquisition, cross-border and domestic money transfers, and e-money issuance services to its client base. The same announcement said Tazapay had closed Series A funding of $16.9 million.
Both companies said the transaction is expected to close in 2027, subject to customary closing conditions and receipt of regulatory approvals, including approval from the Monetary Authority of Singapore. Tazapay said it will continue to operate as it does today until the transaction closes and afterward.

title: Lisa Jacobs to step down as Funding Circle CEO
content:
Lisa Jacobs to step down as Funding Circle CEO
Funding Circle Holdings plc (LON:FCH) today announced that Lisa Jacobs has informed the Board of her intention to step down as CEO, by no later than September 2027.
Lisa Jacobs joined Funding Circle in 2012 and was appointed CEO in January 2022.
The Board will commence a formal search for Lisa’s successor. In the meantime, Ms Jacobs will continue in role, delivering against the Company’s attractive growth and strategic plans, and will work closely with the Board to ensure a smooth and orderly transition.
Ken Stannard, Chair said:
“Although she is not leaving us for some time, on behalf of the Board and all our Circlers, I want to thank Lisa for her outstanding and ongoing contribution to Funding Circle. She has transformed the business, advanced our mission and built a great team. When she joined in 2012, Funding Circle was a start-up built on a simple conviction: that technology could transform how small businesses access finance. Since then, we’ve extended more than £18 billion in credit to more than 135,000 SMEs, and delivered the transformation plan set out in March 2024 to build a simpler, high growth and more profitable business.
“We will be very sorry to say goodbye to Lisa, but we also appreciate that 14 years is a long time. We respect her decision and how she has chosen this timing to coincide with the strong momentum of the business. Lisa is determined to leave Funding Circle in the strongest position possible and ensure a smooth transition. The Board and I are fully focused on finding the right candidate who will build on our strong platform for growth.ˮ
Lisa Jacobs, CEO, said:
“I have loved being part of Funding Circle’s growth story over the last 14 years. I’m privileged to work alongside such a great team of talented and dedicated Circlers. I’m proud of what we have achieved together for the business, Circlers and the small businesses we have backed up and down the country.
“Today’s results show that the business is in the best position that it has ever been. We have shown strong growth and profitability and great foundations for the future – and now feels like the right time to start the process of handing over the reins.
“This is a brilliant business with an important mission. I’m confident the best is yet to come and I remain fully committed to delivering against our attractive growth plans and, when the time comes, ensuring a smooth transition to my successor.”
