title: NBFC funding must diversify as sector grows
content:
NBFC funding: The old description of non-banking financial companies as lenders at the edges of Indian finance is out of date. RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu put numbers to their rise on September 3. NBFC credit is now about 16.7% of nominal GDP, up from 15.9% a year earlier, and is equivalent to roughly 27% of the credit extended by scheduled commercial banks. The larger the sector becomes, the greater the consequences if its funding comes under stress. That is why Murmu’s warning on liquidity deserves attention.
The warning does not come from a sector in distress. The RBI’s June 2026 Financial Stability Report describes NBFCs as resilient, with strong capitalisation and declining asset impairment. Gross non-performing assets were 2.4% at end-March 2026 and the capital adequacy ratio was 24.6%. The issue, therefore, is how to make a growing sector less vulnerable to the next bout of market stress.
READ | NBFCs and private credit reshaping India’s finance ecosystem
NBFC liquidity risk has not disappeared
NBFCs perform an economic function that inevitably creates some maturity risk. A lender may finance a house, a truck or a business investment for several years while raising at least part of its money for shorter periods. The extent of this mismatch differs sharply across institutions. Trouble arises when an NBFC has to refinance liabilities during a period when markets have turned risk-averse. A perfectly serviceable loan book does not generate cash quickly enough if large borrowings fall due and refinancing dries up.
India has seen this happen. The IL&FS defaults in 2018 damaged confidence well beyond the company itself. The RBI subsequently recorded liquidity stress and higher borrowing costs across the NBFC sector, followed by a shift towards longer-term borrowing and greater reliance on banks. The lesson from that episode was straightforward: credit quality alone cannot protect a lender whose funding model leaves it exposed to a sudden loss of market access.
Regulation has since become tighter. The RBI strengthened its liquidity-risk framework in 2019, placed greater responsibility on boards and asset-liability committees, and introduced liquidity coverage requirements for specified NBFCs from December 2020. These changes have reduced some of the vulnerabilities exposed by IL&FS. Murmu’s speech suggests that the job is unfinished. Past liquidity episodes, he said, showed the danger of funding concentration and excessive dependence on short-term wholesale money.
Diversification does not require every NBFC to tap every conceivable source of money. It requires a funding model that does not seize up when one important channel closes. Large lenders should be able to draw on bank finance and bond markets according to conditions. Eligible institutions may also use deposits, while securitisation and loan assignments provide another route for converting assets into funding.
A deeper corporate bond market would help, as Murmu argued. But such a market cannot be created by exhorting investors to buy NBFC paper. Investors need adequate disclosure and confidence that governance standards match the complexity of the balance sheet. Funding diversification and governance are therefore connected. An NBFC that wants broader access to market finance has to earn it.
READ | NBFCs expand reach but face rising headwinds
Securitisation should transfer risk
Murmu’s argument on securitisation goes further. For many lenders, securitisation has primarily been a way to obtain liquidity: a pool of loans is sold or repackaged, giving the originator cash that can be used for fresh lending. Used properly, however, securitisation can also distribute credit risk and release capital.
That distinction matters. If an NBFC originates a large pool of vehicle, housing or business loans and retains all of them on its balance sheet, it retains the associated credit risk. Selling a properly structured pool can transfer part of that risk to investors whose portfolios and risk appetite allow them to hold it.
There is an obvious hazard. A lender that expects to sell loans may become less careful about whom it lends to. The RBI’s securitisation rules address this through minimum holding and retention requirements. Originators must retain an economic interest in securitised assets, giving them a continuing stake in how those loans perform. The objective is to allow risk to move without allowing responsibility for underwriting to disappear with it.
This is where India’s securitisation market has to mature. Its usefulness should be judged by whether it produces genuine risk transfer and a wider investor base, rather than by the volume of short-term liquidity it provides to originators. Transparency becomes important here as well. Investors have to understand the loans they are buying and the risks embedded in the pool.
READ | Supply chain finance: RBI tightens the reins on NBFCs
NBFC funding: Growth requires lending discipline
The liability side is only half of an NBFC balance sheet. Murmu also cautioned lenders against allowing faster credit growth to weaken underwriting. The RBI wants stress testing and early-warning systems to improve as balance sheets expand. Technology can help identify signs of borrower stress earlier, especially where lenders have access to richer cash-flow and transaction data. It cannot rescue a loan that should not have been made.
This matters because NBFCs have become important by doing things that conventional banking often finds difficult or expensive. They have built expertise in vehicle finance, affordable housing and infrastructure lending, while specialised lenders have developed businesses around particular industries and borrower groups. Their ability to assess customers outside the conventional collateral-based model is an economic asset. Weak underwriting would destroy that advantage.
India will need more non-bank credit as its economy expands. Banks cannot efficiently serve every borrower or finance every niche on their own. The policy question is how that expansion will be funded and what risks will accompany it. A sector whose credit is already equivalent to more than a quarter of scheduled commercial bank credit cannot base its resilience on the assumption that refinancing markets will always remain open. The stronger NBFCs become in good times, the better placed they will be to keep lending when money becomes scarce.

title: Erving celebrates $14.7M for long-awaited Evergreen Circle housing complex
content:
ERVING — The mood at the Erving Senior & Community Center was jubilant on Thursday afternoon as Juana Matias, secretary of the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities, announced that $14.7 million in state and federal funding will go to Rural Development Inc. to support the Evergreen Circle housing development.
The gathering in Erving was part of a larger announcement by the Healey-Driscoll administration that nearly $278 million in state and federal financing will support 29 developments in 20 municipalities across Massachusetts. This includes state and federal low-income housing tax credits and subsidy financing from the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities.
Erving, in partnership with Rural Development Inc. (RDI), Berkshire Design Group and Austin Design Cooperative, will build 18 one-bedroom apartments for seniors ages 62 and older, and eight multigenerational units, each with two or three bedrooms, along an extension of Care Drive. This will bring senior housing to the community 24 years after the town first identified the need for senior housing in its June 2002 Master Plan.
Matias said the event in Erving was a “tremendous celebration” of the Healey-Driscoll administration’s commitment to building housing across the state.
“Here we are supporting 26 units of intergenerational living that the state has never done before in a community like Erving, and we’re interested in continuing to work with local partners, because it happens locally,” Matias said. “That’s where it first needs to happen.”
Gov. Maura Healey was expected to attend the celebration, but a personal matter prevented her from being there, Matias said. In a statement released prior to her scheduled tour in six communities that are benefiting from this funding, including Northampton in Hampshire County, Healey said the money will support the development of new housing, along with the preservation and rehabilitation of existing housing.
“This is about making sure that Massachusetts is a state where teachers, nurses, firefighters and young people can actually afford to live,” Healey said.
“Communities of every size are stepping up with smart, creative plans to build the homes their residents need,” Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll said in a statement. “These awards will turn underused properties into housing, modernize housing and preserve homes that residents already depend on.”
In Erving, RDI, a nonprofit created by the Franklin County Regional Housing & Redevelopment Authority, received a combined $10.8 million in state and federal low-income housing tax credit allocations, and $3.9 million in subsidy financing from the state Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities. When coupled with previous grants and loans, the latest awards bring RDI’s project budget to $17.4 million.
RDI Executive Director Gina Govoni and Real Estate Project Manager/Housing Development Director Alyssa Larose shared their excitement about the announcement and the visit from state officials. Govoni pointed out how Erving is unique for being a community that earned funding in its first round of applications.
“I think this award shows how well prepared and how well developed it is,” Govoni said, giving credit to her colleague Larose, who is the project lead for Evergreen Circle.
Govoni noted this funding from the state is exclusively for RDI and its role in constructing the housing, while the town of Erving is supporting the underground infrastructure development needed to support the housing. Larose said there is a funding gap of $650,000, and a Housing Choice Grant is being explored to complete the scope of work.
Erving has a $2.4 million grant from the HousingWorks Infrastructure Program for water and sewer infrastructure upgrades, along with an extension of Care Drive that the multigenerational townhouses and senior housing will abut.
Town Administrator Bryan Smith, who was hired in 2016, recalled how he was first introduced to the project while interviewing for his job. Ten years later, he said it “feels amazing” to be part of seeing the project get this far.
“To know that we are here 10 years later, and we’ve finally got all the pieces,” Smith said, citing the right organizing partners, permitting and funding, “we’re at the precipice of construction. This is amazing. It all feels like it’s all come to fruition.”
Before Smith’s tenure, other town officials and residents led the charge for senior housing, and they continue to be involved. Chair of the Senior Housing Committee and Selectboard member William Bembury, who sat on the 2002 Master Planning Committee, said he’s “ecstatic,” but he is also feeling some shock over the realization that, at long last, “this is going to happen.”
When asked how momentum for furthering the housing project has been maintained for more than two decades, Bembury credited the continued support of local and state organizations and their knowledge on how to proceed.
Admittedly, Bembury said he was sad that some seniors moved out of town because they could no longer afford to live in Erving due to the cost of homeownership. Then there’s those who have died before senior housing could become a reality. However, Bembury is looking to the future for those who can make it back to Erving.
“That’s the sad part, but there’s still some folks out there that have an opportunity to come back,” Bembury said about Evergreen Circle. “They’re still with us, and so I hope they take that opportunity on.”

title: Ark Invest Buys $40.8 Million in Block and Circle Shares, Trims Palantir and AMD
content:
Ark Invest Buys $40.8 Million in Block and Circle Shares, Trims Palantir and AMD
Cathie Wood's Ark Invest kicked off September with a notable reshuffling of its actively managed portfolios, pouring roughly $40.8 million into two crypto-adjacent companies while trimming positions in some of its largest technology holdings. The trades, disclosed through the firm's daily reporting, show a clear emphasis on digital payments and stablecoin infrastructure.
On Monday, the investment firm purchased 456,059 shares of Block, the Jack Dorsey-led payments company, worth approximately $37.4 million based on the day's closing price of $82.02. The buying was spread across three of Ark's exchange-traded funds: the Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK), Ark Next Generation Internet ETF (ARKW), and Ark Blockchain & Fintech Innovation ETF (ARKF). Block shares slipped 1.85% in the session, extending a pattern of Ark using pullbacks in the stock to build its position.
The same day, Ark added 35,192 shares of Circle Internet Group, the issuer of the USDC stablecoin, for roughly $3.36 million. Unlike Block, Circle rallied sharply, closing at $95.55, a gain of 9.65% that recovered most of the previous Friday's 7.5% decline. Circle shares have now appreciated 52.6% over the past month.
Ark's latest moves extend a year-long accumulation of crypto-linked equities. In June, the firm bought 236,759 Block shares worth about $17.2 million through ARKK. It followed up in July with a 19,029-share purchase through ARKW and ARKF, and returned to Circle twice that month, buying 220,012 shares worth roughly $13.9 million when the stock traded below $64, then adding another 109,129 shares after the stablecoin issuer received a limited-purpose trust charter from the New York Department of Financial Services.
Block's second-quarter results, released in early August, appear to have reinforced Ark's conviction. The company reported earnings of $1.02 per share on revenue of $6.62 billion, beating Wall Street estimates on both metrics. Gross profit climbed 25% year over year to $3.17 billion, driven by a 31% jump in Cash App gross profit to $1.97 billion and a 13% increase at Square to $1.16 billion. Management raised its full-year gross profit forecast to $12.51 billion, implying 21% growth from 2025, up from a prior projection of $12.33 billion.
Block has also maintained a significant Bitcoin treasury, holding 9,177 BTC valued at approximately $714 million. Bitcoin gained 23.73% during August, while Ethereum rose 31.44%, providing a tailwind for companies with direct exposure to digital assets. The company joined the S&P 500 in July, replacing Hess Corp. after Chevron completed its acquisition of the oil producer.
The bullish case for Circle got a fresh endorsement last week when Bernstein analysts reiterated an Outperform rating and set a $140 price target. The brokerage cited expanding USDC adoption across stablecoin payments, blockchain-based capital markets, and emerging agentic payment applications. Bernstein noted that USDC supply increased by about $1.7 billion in the preceding week after nearly six months of mostly flat growth. Adjusted stablecoin transaction volume was running at an annualized pace of roughly $17 trillion through July, compared with about $11 trillion during 2025. Circle reported $701 million in second-quarter revenue, up 7% year over year, with USDC circulation reaching $73.3 billion at the end of the period.
Ark's buying was offset by significant sales elsewhere in the portfolio. The firm liquidated 139,456 shares of Palantir Technologies across ARKF, ARKK, and ARKW, a transaction worth roughly $26 million based on the stock's $186.38 close. The divestment came despite Palantir's strong second-quarter report, which showed revenue of $1.94 billion against analyst expectations of $1.80 billion and adjusted earnings of 41 cents per share, exceeding the 35-cent consensus.
Ark also reduced its AMD exposure, selling 8,623 shares through ARKF for approximately $4.1 million based on a closing price of $470.72. The sale continues a pattern of trimming the chipmaker's position in recent weeks, even as AMD announced an expansion of its AI infrastructure initiatives in Saudi Arabia through partnerships with Cisco Systems and HUMAIN.
Additional trades disclosed Monday included the sale of 55,314 Shopify shares through ARKF and 24,867 through ARKW, the sale of 58,873 Roblox shares via ARKF, and purchases of 56,987 Guardant Health shares through ARKG and 200,303 Rocket Lab shares through ARKK. Ark also sold 175,841 shares of Personalis through ARKG.
Ark's portfolio rules generally prevent any single holding from exceeding 10% of a fund's total value, forcing the firm to rebalance as stock prices move. The latest trades suggest a deliberate rotation toward companies positioned at the intersection of payments, blockchain infrastructure, and digital assets, while reducing exposure to AI software and semiconductor names that have delivered substantial gains this year.
Institutional interest in crypto-linked equities has intensified as digital asset prices climbed through August. Ark's decisions to route its conviction through publicly traded companies rather than direct token purchases mirrors a broader trend among traditional asset managers seeking regulated exposure to the sector's growth. Whether the firm continues to add to Block and Circle in the coming weeks will depend on price action and any shift in the fundamental outlook for payments and stablecoin adoption.

title: Sam Bankman-Fried Circle's Anthropic Shares Sold Before Value Exploded
content:
Nishad Singh and Caroline Ellison gave up personal Anthropic shares after the FTX fraud case, but those shares didn't follow Sam Bankman-Fried's bankruptcy stake. They went through the federal forfeiture system, and nobody outside that process yet knows exactly where the money landed.
Anthropic's paper value has turned an old FTX investment into a very current fight over who should benefit from one of the fastest climbs in private tech. The numbers are startling. Anthropic said on May 28, 2026, that it raised $65 billion at a $965 billion post-money valuation. Business Insider reported on August 31 that seized Anthropic shares once owned by two Bankman-Fried associates could now be worth billions.
The clean version is simple. Bankman-Fried's Anthropic stake and his lieutenants' personal stakes were not the same asset, and they didn't move through the same legal pipe.
Bankman-Fried's stake belonged to the FTX bankruptcy estate after the exchange collapsed in November 2022. Singh and Ellison's shares were forfeited in criminal proceedings after they pleaded guilty and cooperated with prosecutors. If you blur those two paths together, you get the wrong story.
The FTX stake was sold in bankruptcy
Bankman-Fried, Nishad Singh and Caroline Ellison each invested in Anthropic's 2022 Series B round, according to court records reviewed by Business Insider. Bankman-Fried bought $500 million worth, which represented 13.56% of Anthropic at the time. Singh acquired $40 million in shares, and Ellison acquired $10 million.
Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the American A.I. Sovereign Wealth Fund Act, proposing a one-time 50 percent equity tax on OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI that would give the federal government board seats and voting shares. The bill dropped the same day Anthropic confidentially filed for an IPO, forcing the industry to treat legislative risk as a... - how to price a SaaS product for enterprise - cold email template that gets replies from investors
That first number is the one most people remember because it sat inside the wreckage of FTX. The shares tied to Bankman-Fried were owned through Clifton Bay, an entity affiliated with Alameda Research, and later landed in bankruptcy court with the rest of the estate's recovered assets.
The estate did what bankrupt estates usually do. It sold.
In March 2024, FTX struck deals to sell most of its Anthropic stake for $884 million. Bloomberg reported that ATIC Third International Investment Company, an entity associated with Abu Dhabi's Mubadala, agreed to buy close to $500 million of the shares, while Jane Street, HOF Capital and Fidelity-managed funds were also among the buyers. A later sale of the remaining shares brought in about $452 million, putting the estate's total Anthropic proceeds near $1.3 billion.
That was a strong recovery by any normal standard. FTX had put in roughly $500 million and more than doubled its money in bankruptcy. But Anthropic stopped being a normal private-company story a long time ago.
The personal shares took a different route
Singh and Ellison's shares were handled as criminal forfeiture, not ordinary bankruptcy property. Business Insider reported that a federal judge ordered their Anthropic shares transferred to the government, with Ellison's shares moving in February 2025 and Singh's in April 2025.
Those shares were then sold to existing Anthropic investors by the U.S. Marshals Service, according to Business Insider. The important part is what remains unknown: the agency hasn't disclosed the buyers, the sale price, the exact timing, or whether the proceeds have gone to FTX victims.
That's not a small detail. Business Insider reported that the FTX estate had received $638 million from Justice Department-seized assets by the end of 2025, mostly from Robinhood shares once owned by Bankman-Fried, and expected about $400 million more from the government. The proceeds from Singh and Ellison's Anthropic shares did not appear to have reached the estate by the end of June 2026, according to the same report.
BitGo CEO Mike Belshe publicly loaded 100 BTC, worth about $6.3 million, into a BitGo wallet and dared Anthropic's Claude to steal it, days after Anthropic disclosed that Claude models broke out of test sandboxes and attacked real companies. The challenge has no formal rules or deadline, and Anthropic has not responded. - how to secure AI agents safely - poorly governed autonomous agents access risk
Frankly, that is the live issue. Not whether the government briefly held a stake in Anthropic, and not whether Bankman-Fried missed out on an AI jackpot. He is serving a 25-year sentence after his 2023 conviction, and the bankruptcy estate already sold the corporate Anthropic position to repay creditors.
The harder question is whether the forfeited personal stakes will reach the same victims. Prosecutors said in court that FTX victim compensation would be handled through remission, a Justice Department process used when a normal restitution system is too unwieldy. With FTX, the number of possible victims ran into the millions.
Anthropic's rise only makes that process look more exposed. The company said its run-rate revenue crossed $47 billion in May 2026, and TechCrunch reported in June that it had confidentially filed for an initial public offering after the $965 billion round. Business Insider also noted that Anthropic has traded on the secondary market at valuations as high as $1.5 trillion.
So yes, the timing stings. Buyers who picked up Anthropic shares from FTX-related sellers in 2024 or 2025 may now be sitting on enormous gains. The FTX estate still got real money back for creditors, but it sold before Anthropic's value moved from astonishing to absurd.
That doesn't make the sale corrupt. It makes it final. The open question is narrower and more concrete: when the federal government sold Singh and Ellison's forfeited shares, how much cash did it collect, and when will FTX's victims see it?

title: BÖRSE
content:
Siemens Energy's Omterra Auction: Five Private Equity Suitors Circle the Turbine Unit
Published on 08/28/2026 at 21:31 | Editorial boerse-global.de
The machinery of corporate separation is already grinding into motion at Siemens Energy, even as the market's attention zeroes in on a far messier question: what price will the market ultimately put on the industrial carve-out, and how much of that value stays with existing shareholders?
Bloomberg reports that the Munich-based group has drafted Goldman Sachs to run a sale process for a majority stake in its Transformation of Industry (ToI) unit — the steam turbine and industrial business that will operate under the name Omterra. CVC, EQT, Bain, Brookfield and KKR are all said to be circling as potential buyers, with the legal and operational separation already underway.
The stakes are considerable. ToI generated €5.7 billion in revenue last fiscal year, according to Reuters, while the Wall Street Journal has cited figures of $6.66 billion for fiscal 2025 at an 11.3 percent margin. Consensus projections for fiscal 2026 point to comparable growth of 5 to 7 percent and a margin between 11 and 13 percent before special items.
The valuation tug-of-war
What matters most for Siemens Energy shareholders is the size of the "meaningful minority stake" the company intends to retain. A competitive auction — five private equity names in the mix suggests genuine tension — could push the price higher, strengthening the balance sheet and freeing capital for the grid and power businesses that will form the core of the slimmed-down group. A weak outcome, by contrast, would leave the parent with only a token holding and undermine the entire logic of the restructuring.
The market is already pricing in some uncertainty. Shares changed hands at €149.20 in recent trading, down 1 percent on the day and 2.7 percent on the week. That leaves the stock roughly 24 percent below its April peak of €195.38, though still up 24 percent year-to-date — and a considerable 79 percent above the September 2025 trough. The equity sits 3.6 percent beneath its 50-day moving average of €154.70, a technical signal that near-term momentum has cooled.
A record quarter in the rearview mirror
The divestiture talk arrives on the back of a quarter that underlined the operational turnaround. Third-quarter results, confirmed on August 26, showed revenue up 18.5 percent to €11.45 billion, while adjusted EBITA more than tripled to €1.623 billion from €497 million a year earlier. Even Siemens Gamesa, the wind subsidiary that has been the group's problem child, posted its first positive adjusted EBITA since 2022 at €75 million, reaffirming its target of reaching breakeven in fiscal 2026.
Order intake hit a record €17.9 billion in the quarter, lifting the backlog to €162 billion. The company also flagged a contract from the operator of the Bard Offshore 1 wind farm to modernise frequency converters across 80 turbines from late 2026.
While Siemens Energy navigates a complex industrial carve-out, many UK businesses face their own restructuring headaches — often overlooking a costly compliance gap in workplace safety documentation. Buybacks and analyst divergence
The strategic overhaul is running in parallel with capital returns. Between June 4 and August 14, Siemens Energy repurchased roughly €1 billion of its own shares under the second tranche of its buyback programme.
Analyst opinion splits along predictable lines. JPMorgan reaffirmed "Overweight" with a €245 target on August 26, while Jefferies held "Buy" at €215. Deutsche Bank Research and Bernstein both sit at €210 — "Buy" and "Outperform" respectively — with the latter citing rising power demand from data centres and AI infrastructure as a structural tailwind. RBC trimmed its target from €210 to €200 on August 26 while keeping "Outperform," a sign that even the bulls are tempering their enthusiasm for the transaction's outcome. The broader consensus across 31 analysts lands at €197.62, with 24 houses recommending purchase.

What happens next
The immediate catalyst is the auction itself. Should multiple bidders table binding offers, the competitive dynamic could work in Siemens Energy's favour. But private equity processes are notoriously fluid, and the unresolved question of the final ownership structure — majority sale, eventual capital markets listing, or some hybrid — leaves room for slippage.
The next formal checkpoint arrives on November 11, when the group reports fourth-quarter and full-year results. By then, the shape of the Omterra transaction — and whether the promised "meaningful minority stake" materialises at a valuation that justifies the restructuring — should be considerably clearer.

title: Circle U. project receives Erasmus+ funding to educate future leaders in sustainable health
content:
With EUR 400,000 in Erasmus+ funding, the Sustainable Health Sciences & Humanities project will establish a master's-level Honours Certificate in Sustainable Health. Led by the University of Oslo in partnership with Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin and the University of Belgrade, the initiative will equip students to address complex challenges at the intersection of health, the environment and public policy.
Strengthening Circle U.'s educational portfolio
The proposal received an impressive score of 90 out of 100 points. Evaluators highlighted the partners' extensive experience within Circle U., noting that this provides a strong foundation for successful implementation.
By combining Oslo’s expertise in planetary health, Berlin’s leadership in systems thinking and ecology, and Belgrade’s competence in One Health and toxicology, the project creates a learning environment that no single institution could provide alone.
Innovative pedagogy and Artificial Intelligence
The certificate consists of three course packages (5 ECTS each), distributed across the partner universities. Students will utilise cutting-edge digital tools, including:
- A digital sandbox: a virtual environment for interactive, problem-based collaboration.
- Datathons: intensive workshops where students use AI and other digital tools to analyse large datasets, policy documents and media narratives.
- Responsible AI practices: training in the ethical and critical use of AI when developing solutions to complex health and environmental challenges.
Transnational collaboration and real-world impact
While much of the teaching is digital to minimise the carbon footprint, the project emphasises social and academic community building across borders. A central feature is the Blended Intensive Programme (BIP), culminating in a five-day student conference and hackathon in Belgrade. Here, students from across the alliance will present their solutions to experts from industry, NGOs, and the public sector.
Long-term vision
The project aims for 80 students to complete the certificate during the 36-month funding period. Additionally, a "Train the Trainer" module will be developed to train 30–40 educators in sustainability pedagogy, ensuring these innovative methods persist within the alliance well beyond the project's conclusion in 2029.
Through this initiative, Circle U. takes a significant step towards breaking down academic silos and strengthening European higher education, creating a truly integrated learning experience that equips students to address complex sustainability and health challenges.
About the project funding
- The project Sustainable Health Sciences & Humanities is funded under Key Action 2 (KA220) Cooperation Partnerships, which supports transnational cooperation, innovation and exchange of practices between organisations across Europe.
- KA220 is a decentralised action, meaning proposals are submitted to and managed by national Erasmus+ agencies rather than directly by the European Commission.
- Cooperation Partnerships typically bring together at least three organisations or higher education institutions from three different Erasmus+ programme countries.
- Projects may receive lump-sum grants of €120,000, €250,000 or €400,000, depending on the scope and ambition of the project.
- Universities, research organisations, NGOs, public authorities and other eligible institutions can apply through annual Erasmus+ calls.

title: Full Circle completes acquisition of Mac of All Trades
content:
Full Circle Electronics is beefing up its Apple-related ITAD and e-recycling capabilities, acquiring one of the world’s largest Apple refurbishers.
Full Circle closed on its acquisition of Mac of All Trades in mid-August. The deal will see Full Circle operate the company, which has handled second-hand Apple electronics since 1995.
Mac of All Trades will retain its name while helping bolster Full Circle’s Apple capabilities, Full Circle CEO Dave Daily said. Work on the deal began when Mac of All Trades reached out about a potential acquisition in the spring, said Daily, who declined to share the financial terms. Given the consistent demand for Apple products and the value they retain, the opportunity was not one to pass up, he said.
“We felt their expertise in the Apple ecosystem could be very valuable,” he said. “We felt it would be complementary to our customers.”
Daily spent Monday in Mac of All Trades’ Tampa headquarters meeting its 40 employees — all of whom will be kept on for the foreseeable future; CEO Michael Snyder will be among them, with Daily saying he plans to stay on board for 12-18 months.
Work at the 25,000-square-foot Mac of All Trades will continue as normal, Daily said — for employees and customers alike. Initial plans are to look for potential operational efficiencies, he said, while sending some of the Apple products received at Full Circle sites to Tampa for processing, given the institutional knowledge of that platform within the building. Long term, Full Circle may take some of that knowledge to apply to its two main ITAD facilities in Chicago and the Bay Area.
“Any time you do an acquisition, there has to be some thought of synergies and mutual growth,” he said. “It is a really well-run, clean, organized facility. Full Circle does have some nice tech, things we are working on with our systems that could be beneficial to them from an IT standpoint … and hopefully we can bring them in more business through our bigger footprint.”
Daily said continued growth within the ITAD industry makes this move a natural progression. Full Circle will consider any acquisitions or other growth should it make sense, he said.
“With AI influencing refresh cycles, with the growth in general of ITAD and e-recycling, the need to create some scale to invest in technologies — we think that now is the ideal time to be investing in ITAD and our business,” he said. “When you look at companies to acquire, the biggest variable is the culture, is it a good cultural fit. That’s one thing we definitely have with Mac of All Trades.”
Prior to this transaction, Arizona-based Full Circle operated 10 sites in six states, as well as Mexico and Colombia. It’s one of nearly two dozen companies owned by San Diego-based Tide Rock Holdings.
Earlier this month, Full Circle unveiled its new customer portal at the ITAD Summit in Las Vegas. The streamlined platform was designed to track assets in real time, generate customized reports and review financial details.

title: Cathie Wood Defends Circle Stake After 42% Slide, Says Wall Street Can't Grasp Stablecoin Disruptor
content:
Cathie Wood Defends Circle Stake After 42% Slide, Says Wall Street Can't Grasp Stablecoin Disruptor
Cathie Wood pushed back against Wall Street's skepticism toward Circle Internet Group Inc. (CRCL) over the weekend, arguing that analysts who built their careers covering legacy payment networks are structurally incapable of valuing the stablecoin issuer.
The ARK Invest founder was responding Sunday to a chart posted by analyst Alex Obchakevich that compared one-year share performance across Visa Inc. (V), Mastercard Inc. (MA) and Circle. Visa rose roughly 5% over the period, Mastercard was approximately flat, and Circle fell 42%.
Wood acknowledged the divergence but reframed it as evidence of market failure rather than company weakness. "Though CRCL has appreciated 84% since its IPO, this one-year chart illustrates the inefficiency of public equity markets in the short term," she wrote. "Many financial services analysts have built their long-term track records off of $V and $MA and cannot fathom Circle, the disrupter."
Her arithmetic on the IPO gain was off, however. Circle priced its June 2025 float at $31 per share and closed Friday at $87.98, a gain of roughly 184%, not 84% as Wood claimed.
She then reached for historical precedent. Mastercard has appreciated roughly 150 times since its 2006 listing, she said, while Visa has gained about 33 times since its 2008 IPO. The implication: analysts who looked prescient recommending those stocks were riding a technological wave, and Circle represents the next one. Both multiples check out against adjusted share prices and Friday closes.
Circle went public on June 5, 2025, pricing at $31. The stock opened at $69, up about 123%, and closed its first session at $83.23, a gain of about 168%. Since then it has been volatile, reflecting broader uncertainty about how markets should value stablecoin issuers.
ARK Invest's conviction is not rhetorical. The firm held $481.43 million worth of CRCL shares across its ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK), ARK Next Generation Internet ETF (ARKW) and ARK Blockchain & Fintech Innovation ETF (ARKF) as of the latest disclosures. The flagship ARKK fund alone held 3,931,968 shares on Friday, worth $329 million and representing 5.14% of the portfolio, making Circle the largest crypto bet in the fund, ahead of Coinbase.
Wall Street's view of Circle is far from settled. Of 21 analysts covering the stock, 11 rate it a strong buy and two a buy, while five say hold and three say sell. Price targets range from $37 to $173, a 4.7-fold gap that underscores the absence of a shared valuation framework. The average target sits at $98.61.
The dispersion reflects genuine complexity in Circle's business model. The company issues USDC, a dollar-pegged stablecoin backed by cash and short-term U.S. government debt. Much of its revenue comes from interest earned on those reserves, making it sensitive to rate movements. Revenue grew about 37% in the most recent quarter and the company posted a surprise profit in early August, yet its market value still fell 30%.
Competition adds another layer of uncertainty. Circle is building a four-layer financial stack on its Arc blockchain, while Open USD, a consortium of more than 140 firms, is pursuing similar infrastructure for tokenized dollars. Regulatory frameworks for stablecoins remain in flux across jurisdictions, with legislative clarity still pending in the United States.
Circle shares closed 5.16% higher at $87.98 on Friday, then slipped 1.16% in Monday's pre-market trading.
Wood's pattern of accumulating positions through steep drawdowns is well established, with prior concentrated bets in electric vehicles, genomics and other disruptive sectors. Whether this one resolves in her favor will depend on USDC's market share trajectory, the interest rate environment and the pace at which stablecoin regulation takes shape.

title: Capital on Tap business credit card: features, fees and alternatives
content:
Capital on Tap business credit card: features, fees and alternatives
Published on: 22nd August 2026
Capital on Tap is one of the better-knownÂ business credit cards in the UK, 1% cashback on everything you spend, with no annual fee on the standard card.
If you're weighing it up, the things worth understanding are how the rewards actually pay out, what the Â£299 Pro tier buys you, the Preloading feature that most business credit cards don't offer, and whether your business will qualify. This guide covers each, then sets the card against the Funding Circle Cashback business credit card so you can see where the two differ.
All Capital on Tap product details below are taken from itsÂ business credit cards pageÂ andÂ cashback page, correct as of August 2026. Rates, fees and terms can change and vary by circumstances, so it's worth confirming the latest details directly with Capital on Tap before applying.
What is the Capital on Tap business credit card?
It's a Visa business credit card from Capital on Tap.
- You get a credit limit of up to Â£250,000, set on your circumstances, and you spend against it like any other business credit card.Â
- Rates start from 13.86% APR (variable), and Capital on Tap states that clearing your balance in full each month means you pay no interest at all.
Alongside the card sit the things most card-first providers now offer: unlimited free employee cards with individual spend limits, virtual cards for online spending, no foreign exchange fees, accounting software syncing, and a mobile app.Â
How the rewards work
You earn 1 point for every Â£1 you spend, which works out at 1% cashback. There's no cap, no spending categories to track, and no introductory period to keep an eye on. Points become available as soon as a purchase clears.
Where Capital on Tap differs from a straight cashback card is what you can do with those points. You can:
- Take them as cash into your business bank account
- Use them to reduce your card balance
- Convert them to Avios with The British Airways Club or Qatar Airways Privilege Club
- Convert them to Virgin Points or Radisson Rewards
- Spend them on gift cards from retailers including Amazon, John Lewis and Tesco
The trade-off is that it's a system you have to actively engage with, rather than cashback that simply lands.
How cashback and reward points are treated in your accounts depends on how your business is structured, and HMRC guidance differs by case. Speak to your accountant or a qualified tax adviser before you factor rewards into a budget.
The two tiers of Capital on Tap credit card
How does Preloading work?
Preloading lets you top up your Capital on Tap card with your own money and spend that before you touch your credit limit. It still earns cashback at the standard rate.
The practical use is a purchase that exceeds your limit. Rather than applying for an increase, you fund the gap yourself. It's an unusual feature for a business credit card, and it effectively lets the card double as a prepaid facility when you want it to.
Who can apply
Capital on Tap asks that:
- You're an active UK director, or a shareholder with 25% or more of the business
- The business is registered as an Ltd, LLP or PLC, and listed as active on Companies House
- There are no unsatisfied CCJs against you or the business in the last 12 months
- The business isn't in an industry Capital on Tap classes as high risk
Sole traders aren't accepted, and nor are charities, trusts, funds, Royal Charters or dormant companies.
You'll need your personal details, the business's registered name, address and company number, your average monthly turnover, and bank details for settling the card. Capital on Tap says decisions take around 2 minutes, with virtual card access straight away and a physical card in 2 to 5 business days.
Does applying affect your credit score?
Capital on Tap runs a soft search on you personally, which doesn't affect your personal credit score, alongside a business credit check. I
Like most UK business credit cards, it requires a personal guarantee from a director. That means if the business can't pay, you're personally responsible for the debt, so card activity can affect your personal credit position if things go wrong. It's a binding commitment, and it's worth taking independent legal advice before signing one.
Used in the right way, a business credit card helps build a commercial credit history that lenders look at when you come to borrow. Used badly, the same mechanism works against you.
How it compares with the Funding Circle Cashback business credit card
There are three key differences worth noting:
- The shape of the cashback:Â Both land on 1% uncapped long term. Funding Circle front-loads the first 6 months at 2%; Capital on Tap pays 1% from the first pound with nothing to expire. Which suits you depends on when your spending happens.
- What you do with what you earn:Â Capital on Tap gives you points with several exits, including travel conversions. Funding Circle credits cashback to your balance automatically, with nothing to redeem or convert.
- Eligibility:Â Capital on Tap takes LLPs and PLCs and sets no minimum trading period, but wants you to hold a business bank account. Funding Circle's card is for UKÂ limited companiesÂ trading at least a year with turnover of Â£30,000 or more.
Fees, rates and features vary between providers and change over time. Check current terms on each provider's own site and compare them against your own numbers rather than a headline. Our guide toÂ business credit card rates, fees and chargesÂ sets out what to look at.
Alternatives worth comparing
If travel points and tiered perks matter less to you than cashback landing in your account without any admin, theÂ Funding Circle Cashback business credit cardÂ gives you best-in-business cashback with none of the usual fees.

There's no need to switch your business banking.Â Check your eligibility online in minutes and get an instant decision.Â Only limited companies can apply without affecting their credit score.Â
If the pressure point is a specific large bill rather than everyday spend,Â FlexiPayÂ may suit you better. No. It accepts Ltds, LLPs and PLCs. Charities, trusts, funds, Royal Charters and dormant companies aren't eligible either.

Capital on Tap runs a soft search on you personally plus a business credit check, and notes business checks are visible to other lenders. With Funding Circle, only limited companies can check eligibility without affecting their credit score.

title: Yahoo Finance
content:
Circle Internet (NYSE:CRCL) shares jumped 6.0% in pre-market trading on Friday, extending their recent rally after the company announced the acquisition of a significant portion of IBM's global blockchain patent portfolio.
The transaction covers more than 680 patent families and almost 1,000 issued patents, considerably expanding Circle's intellectual property holdings as it seeks to strengthen its position across stablecoins and blockchain infrastructure.
The deal was announced on August 20 and initially lifted Circle shares by around 2% in pre-market trading. Momentum has continued into Friday's session, with the stock climbing to $88.70 from its previous close of $83.66.
IBM patents strengthen Circle's blockchain technology position
Investors have interpreted the acquisition primarily as a strategic investment in Circle's underlying technology capabilities rather than a financial transaction.
By acquiring a substantial collection of IBM blockchain patents, Circle gains access to intellectual property covering technologies that could complement its existing digital asset infrastructure and reinforce its longer-term competitive position.
The scale of the portfolio has helped generate renewed interest in the shares as investors assess how Circle could use the patents to support future products and infrastructure.
Regulatory developments provide additional support
The company has also benefited from an improving regulatory backdrop for the US cryptocurrency industry.
A revised version of the Senate Republican Clarity Act introduces tighter provisions surrounding government-issued digital tokens while leaving private-sector cryptocurrency companies such as Circle outside those direct restrictions.
The changes have added to expectations that greater regulatory clarity could create a more predictable operating environment for established digital asset companies.
Analyst sentiment has provided further support, with bullish price targets from Bernstein and JPMorgan continuing to underpin expectations around Circle's longer-term prospects.
Coinbase's renewal of its USDC partnership with Circle has also reinforced confidence in the competitive position of the company's flagship stablecoin.
Bitcoin rally boosts crypto-linked stocks
The wider environment for cryptocurrency-related equities has also turned increasingly supportive.
Bitcoin's advance above $71,600 has strengthened sentiment across the digital asset sector, while falling Treasury yields following the US Treasury's expansion of its bond-buyback programme have helped increase appetite for riskier assets.

title: Circle and Coinbase Are Turning ‘Boring’ Stablecoins Into Great News for Investors
content:
Listen to the audio version of this article (generated by AI).
Key Points
- Stablecoins are becoming an increasingly ordinary part of the financial system’s infrastructure, and that shift toward mainstream adoption is creating a new investment case.
- Circle and Coinbase offer different ways to invest in the same stablecoin ecosystem, with both positioned to benefit from the new GENIUS Act regulatory framework.
- Real-world stablecoin usage remains small but is doubling, while clearer regulation could encourage banks, payment companies, and large businesses to accelerate adoption.
Shares of Circle Internet Group (CRCL) and Coinbase (COIN) both moved higher on Monday after the Treasury Department proposed new rules for the GENIUS Act, the stablecoin law enacted in July 2025. The proposal will be open to public comment for 60 days, with a final rule expected before January 2027.
Although stablecoins won’t suddenly become mainstream simply because the Treasury Department published its proposal, something more important has already happened.
Stablecoins are getting boring.
For most of crypto’s history, that would have sounded like an insult. Now, it may be stablecoins’ investment case.
The original crypto pitch involved overthrowing banks, replacing currencies, and cutting out financial intermediaries. Stablecoins are turning into something much less dramatic – a form of payments infrastructure. Mastercard (MA) is building around them. Payments app MoneyGram uses them. Businesses can settle payments at midnight on a Sunday instead of waiting for the banking system to open.
In short, stablecoins are becoming part of our ordinary world.
The GENIUS Act’s Impact on Stablecoins and Crypto Stocks
That leaves investors with a more useful question than whether crypto is “the future.” The question now is: If stablecoins become ordinary financial plumbing, who gets paid for it?
Circle and Coinbase have two very different answers…
A stablecoin such as Circle’s USDC is a digital dollar that can move across blockchain networks at any hour. The useful part of that idea has little to do with a person buying a cup of coffee… Electronic payment networks such as Mastercard and Visa (V) already handle those types of transactions just fine.
The bigger opportunity is where the existing system gets expensive or slow. Again, with traditional finance, those drawbacks happen with things like cross-border payments, remittances, corporate treasury, and settlement outside banking hours.
On stablecoin rails, the payment and settlement can become the same event rather than a message followed by money moving a day or two later. The hope is to fix these inefficiencies.
That gets us to Circle.
Circle issues USDC and holds reserves against those coins. It earns interest on the reserves it holds. In the second quarter, reserve income was $667.7 million, or 95.2% of Circle’s total revenue. Average USDC in circulation reached about $76.5 billion, up from $61 billion a year earlier.
The attraction is obvious. If more businesses and consumers use USDC, Circle gets more dollars to hold in reserve and potentially more reserve income.
But there’s a catch.
Circle’s economics depend heavily on interest rates. Lower rates mean lower returns on those reserves. Circle’s own filing estimates that a one-percentage-point decline in rates, if USDC circulation remains constant, would cut annual reserve income by roughly $737 million.
Then there’s Coinbase.
Coinbase is fascinating because it sits on the other side of Circle’s economics. It distributes USDC and gets paid handsomely for doing it.
Circle paid Coinbase $324.6 million in distribution costs in the second quarter alone. Coinbase says its customers held a total of $20 billion in USDC in Coinbase Products, on average, during the quarter – more than 30% of the total supply of USDC.
Coinbase captured roughly half of all USDC economics (meaning the yield earned by the investments USDC holds and who benefits from it) over the past year.
That gives investors two very different stocks tied to the same trend.
Circle makes more money when USDC circulation and reserve income grow… while Coinbase gets a large piece of the economics for putting USDC in front of customers.
Stablecoins also give Coinbase something it badly wants: revenue that doesn’t require customers to trade bitcoin constantly. Subscription and services revenue reached $555 million last quarter, or 48% of net revenue.
The Next Test for Stablecoins Is Real-World Use
There’s plenty of room for stablecoins to disappoint, however.
Most stablecoin activity still has little to do with buying goods or paying workers. The figures I have been watching put actual payments at roughly $390 billion out of about $35 trillion in stablecoin-network activity over a recent 12-month period (annualized for 2025 in December). Call it 1%. Trading, arbitrage, and machines moving liquidity still dominate the industry.
I keep coming back to the other side of that number, though.
The payments portion is tiny, but it more than doubled from 2024 to 2025.
The GENIUS Act will not make stablecoins mainstream by itself. The Treasury cannot force people to use USDC. What stablecoin regulation can do is remove one of the primary reasons banks, payment companies, and large businesses have hesitated to build around it.
That creates competition, too. Circle and Coinbase will not have this market to themselves.
But the investment question has become much more concrete. We no longer have to ask whether blockchain will someday find a use beyond crypto trading.
Money is already moving over these networks, and we’ll soon get to find out who exactly stands to gain when stablecoins become part of the main financial plumbing.
Good investing,
Eric Wade
Editor’s Note: Whitney Tilson … hedge fund legend, Harvard grad, and the investor CNBC called “The Prophet” … just stepped forward not just as a financial expert, but as a father and an American. He says we’re entering the most chaotic six months this country has seen in a generation. The signs are already everywhere. And he believes most people have no idea what’s coming for their money. title: KKR to pick up stake in entertainment ticketing platform BookMyShow

Global private equity firm KKR will acquire a minority stake in online ticketing and event management platform BookMyShow, as the Indian company looks to scale its live entertainment business and deepen its full-stack entertainment offerings.
Neither KKR nor BookMyShow disclosed any financial terms of the transaction in a joint statement.
However, Reuters cited a source as saying that KKR will buy a stake of about 6% for $40 million to $50 million. It added that the deal implies an estimated valuation of $667 million to $833 million for BookMyShow.
BookMyShow, operated by Bigtree Entertainment Pvt. Ltd, made early inroads into technology-enabled entertainment experiences in India when it began operations in 2007. Since then, it has evolved from a ticketing platform into a full-stack entertainment company with offerings across movies, live entertainment and experiences.
The company, which is backed by Jungle Ventures, TPG, Accel, Elevation Capital, and Reliance Industries unit Network18, is present in over 700 towns and cities in India with partnerships across the entertainment industry.
Akshay Tanna, partner and head of India private equity at KKR, said the PE firm would support BookMyShow in its next phase of growth in “India’s out-of-home entertainment sector”.
“We believe BookMyShow will play an important role in advancing India’s ambition to become a global entertainment hub and a premier destination for leading artists and acts from around the world,” Tanna said.
Ashish Hemrajani, founder and CEO, BookMyShow, cited KKR’s global perspective, deep expertise and strong understanding of consumer businesses as invaluable aspects for their next growth phase.
“The timing of this investment is particularly exciting, as we have significantly expanded our presence across the live entertainment landscape and are seeing the opportunity for India’s entertainment economy to grow like never before,” Hemrajani said.
Some of BookMyShow’s live entertainment experiential shows in the past few years include Lollapalooza India, U2’s The Joshua Tree Tour, NBA’s debut games in India, Disney’s Aladdin, Cirque du Soleil BAZZAR, shows by international artists such as Coldplay, Ed Sheeran, Travis Scott, Linkin’ Park, John Mayer, Guns N’ Roses, Post Malone, Def Leppard, Justin Bieber among others.
BookMyShow also offers cinema and live ticketing, organic reviews, and BookMyShow Stream (TVOD), a home-grown transactional video-on-demand platform.
For KKR, this marks an addition to its list of transactions so far in India, including Medicover India, Lighthouse Learning, Vini Cosmetics, Healthcare Global Enterprises, Darwinbox, and Rebel Foods.
KKR’s global media and entertainment investments include ByteDance, Epic Games, Simon & Schuster, Internet Brands, Chord Music Partners, PlayOnSports, OverDrive, and Superstruct.
The investment banking arm of Avendus was the financial adviser to the transaction. Trilegal acted as legal advisor. The transaction is subject to regulatory approvals

title: Peak XV, Together Fund join Wispr Flow’s $280 mn funding round
content:
US-based AI voice startup Wispr Flow has raised $280 million in Series B funding at a $2 billion valuation, with India-focused venture capital firms Peak XV Partners and Together Fund among the new investors in the round.
The round was led by existing investor Menlo Ventures and saw participation from existing backers Notable Capital, NEA, Neo Ventures, 8VC and MVP Ventures. New investors included Acrew, Activate, Forerunner, Goodwater, Peak XV, Together Fund and PLUS Capital, along with a group of athletes, artists and cultural leaders, the startup said in a statement.
The fundraise brings Wispr Flow's total capital raised to $361 million and comes less than a year after its previous round, which valued the company at about $700 million.
Founded in 2021 by Stanford graduates Tanay Kothari and Sahaj Garg, Wispr Flow develops an AI-powered voice dictation tool that allows users to speak into applications and workflows instead of typing. Its Flow product converts speech into polished text and is used across professional and enterprise workflows.
Peak XV has been increasing its investments in US-based AI and software startups as part of a broader push beyond India. It recently led a $50 million round in US-based voice AI startup Vapi and has backed overseas companies including Primer, Exaforce, PostHog, MarqVision and Hyperbound.
Alongside the fundraise, Wispr Flow has launched Canto, its first proprietary speech model. The company said the model can reduce word error rates in difficult conditions from more than 30% to between 5% and 10%. It also plans to use the fresh capital to further develop its speech technology and expand its products.
Wispr Flow said its users have now generated more than 60 billion words through the platform. The company is also used by employees at almost all Fortune 500 companies and more than 10,000 enterprises.

title: NeoGeoInfo, Rezolv, LISSUN, Atravelq pocket early-stage funding
content:
Spatial intelligence startup NeoGeoInfo Technologies, lending technology company Rezolv, health-tech firm LISSUN, and travel company Atravelq have secured funding in separate early-stage rounds, the companies said on Tuesday.
NeoGeoInfo Technologies
Gurugram-headquartered NeoGeoInfo Technologies has raised $20 million (Rs 191 crore) in a Series A round from Neev II Fund and Aavishkaar Capital, the investment arm of Aavishkaar Group.
NeoGeo was founded in 2019 by Sreeramam GV and Brahmam GVS. It provides integrated spatial intelligence solutions to government and corporate clients across natural resource management, disaster management, urban governance, utilities, infrastructure, and smart cities. The company offers data acquisition—using satellite imagery, LiDAR, drones, and ground surveys—through data processing, AI/ML-driven analytics, and tech-enabled industry-specific software platforms.
The company said the fresh capital will be deployed to deepen its platform and product portfolio through investment in R&D and technical capabilities, expand into international markets in the Middle East and the Americas, and strengthen its team to serve a growing pipeline of large, technically complex projects.
ICICI Securities acted as the exclusive financial advisor on the transaction.
Rezolv, a lending technology platform for financial services, has raised $12.5 million in its Series A round led by Norwest. The round also saw participation from Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia and India, and existing investor 3one4 Capital.
The capital will be used to strengthen Rezolv's core AI capabilities across the lending suite, including sales, risk, underwriting and collections. The startup is building an end-to-end automation platform for lending workflows and advancing its vision of becoming a category-defining AI platform globally.
Founded in 2024 by Karan Mehta and Sonali Jindal, former founders of Kissht, Rezolv serves banks and NBFCs by pairing a comprehensive debt collection platform with AI, and combining deep lending and collections expertise with an AI-first technology stack. It has partnered with over 22 banks and NBFCs, including AU Small Finance Bank, ICICI Bank, Poonawalla Fincorp, Bajaj Auto Credit, Five-Star Business Finance, Muthoot Capital, Finova Capital, IndoStar, Protium, IIFL, Northern Arc, APAC Financial Services and Vridhi Home Finance, among others.
Single specialty health-tech company LISSIN has closed its Series A funding round with Rs 48 crore ($5 million), led by Colossa Ventures, with participation from Physis Capital and existing investors, including RPSG Capital Ventures, Ivycap Ventures, Rainmatter, Multiply Ventures and SucSEED Ventures.
The round also saw participation from new investors New Age India Fund and Beyond Capital Ventures.
LISSUN operates through its childcare brand, Sunshine by LISSUN, which is building a network of child development centres across India alongside a suite of AI-led platforms and tools.
The startup, which focuses on children with special needs and developmental delays, said it plans to use the capital to expand Sunshine by LISSUN centres in key cities, build AI-led solutions on its proprietary technology and data, and strengthen clinical processes across the network.
Atravelq has secured an undisclosed amount in fresh funding at an equity valuation of Rs 10 crore, backed by its seed investors and founding stakeholders.
The Chandigarh-based travel company, which focuses on personalised international travel, said it will deploy the capital to support its next phase of growth through investments in technology and enhanced customer experience. So far, the company has served more than 10,000 travellers and facilitated close to 6,000 international journeys.
Founded by Prashant Daroch, Atravelq facilitates customised global travel experiences. It provides holiday packages, visa services, flights, hotels, transfers, and concierge services in more than 180 destinations, including Europe, Japan, Southeast Asia, and New Zealand. The company also has an office in the UAE, which supports its international travel business.

title: BÖRSE
content:
Three Tech Giants Circle India's Darwinbox in Pre-IPO Bidding War
Published on 08/18/2026 at 16:41 | Editorial boerse-global.de
The race to acquire Darwinbox, an Indian cloud-based human resources platform backed by private equity firm KKR, has drawn in three of the biggest names in enterprise software. ADP, Microsoft and Salesforce are all reported to be weighing bids for the company, which had been preparing for its own stock market debut.
ADP's interest emerged publicly this week, with sources valuing the target at roughly $1.8 billion to $2 billion. The US payroll and HR services firm is said to have moved early, but it is not alone in its pursuit. Reports indicate that both Microsoft and Salesforce had signalled acquisition interest before Darwinbox could take the IPO route.
The timing is notable. Darwinbox had already laid groundwork for a public listing, and the sudden pile-up of suitors underscores how fiercely the HR technology sector is consolidating. For ADP, absorbing Darwinbox would broaden its portfolio considerably, particularly in Asia-Pacific markets where the Indian firm has built a strong reputation for cloud-native human capital management tools.
Darwinbox's growth metrics help explain the appeal. In its 2025 fiscal year, the company booked revenue of 533.9 crore Indian rupees, a 50 percent jump from the prior year. International markets drove much of that momentum, contributing 63 percent of new sales, with overseas revenue climbing 83 percent. That global footprint makes it an attractive fit for service providers like ADP that are looking to deepen their reach in fast-growing regions.
The company's fundraising history also points to investor confidence. In spring 2026, Darwinbox raised $140 million in a financing round that valued it at $1 billion. To date, it has accumulated $290 million in total capital.
The bidding contest reflects a broader trend across the HR software landscape. As payroll processing becomes more complex and businesses demand integrated workforce management tools, larger players are increasingly looking to buy rather than build. The convergence of ADP's latest payroll research—which highlights operational pressures in wage administration—with its reported acquisition ambitions suggests that market leaders see consolidation as the strategic answer to those challenges.
Who ultimately wins the Darwinbox sweepstakes remains an open question. The valuation expectations, stretching to $2 billion, signal just how much confidence buyers have in the company's future positioning. For now, the attention shifts to whether Darwinbox's management opts for a sale or presses ahead with the IPO it had been planning.

title: Top PEs, strategics circle Actis-owned BluPine Energy for up to $2 bn deal
content:
A clutch of private equity and strategics have expressed interest in BluPine, as UK-based Actis explores a sale of the renewable energy platform, seeking a valuation of about $1.5-2.0 billion, three people familiar with the matter said.
“KKR, NIIF (National Investment and Infrastructure Fund) and Blackstone are closely evaluating the asset, while ISquared Capital is exploring an investment in the company through its clean energy platform HEXA. Inox Clean Energy is also among those spending time on the asset,” one of the people cited above said.
“Others, including Macquarie, RPSG Group, Torrent Power and Apraava Energy, are also in the fray,” a second person said on the condition of anonymity, as the discussions are private. “The binding bids are due in the next 10-12 days,” said a third person in the know, while confirming the above details.
Actis declined to comment on the development. “We don't comment on deal speculation unfortunately,” its spokesperson said. Blackstone, Macquarie and KKR declined to comment, while emails sent to other potential bidders did not elicit a response until press time.
Actis launched BluPine Energy in 2022, targeting 4GW capacity of utility scale solar, wind and storage projects through a buy-and-build strategy with both government and commercial & industrial (C&I) PPAs across India. In the same year, BluPine acquired a 404MW operating pan-Indian solar portfolio as part of its growth.
Led by Neerav Nanavaty, the Gurugram-based firm is among the leading renewable energy service providers that develop, build, own, and operate projects across India to support the country’s clean energy transition. It has rapidly expanded its C&I business by providing customized renewable energy solutions through captive, group captive and open access models, enabling business across sectors achieve their sustainability and decarbonization objectives.
Actis is a major global infrastructure investor with a history of building businesses and operating assets world over. It has deployed more than $7.1 billion to date in Asia, across different strategies. A leading energy investor, it has built or operated over 8GW of installed capacity in the region, including more than 5.5GW of renewables.
Actis invests in structural themes that aim to support long-term, equitable growth in defensive, critical infrastructure across energy transition, digitalization transition, and supply chain transformation, according to its website. Its portfolio assets in India include Stride Climate Investments, Athena Renewable Energy, Sprng Energy, Ostro Energy, and Vindhyachal Expressway Pvt Ltd, some of which it has exited over the years.
The massive scale of India's green energy space has attracted the attention of both Indian and global investors. These investments have gained momentum in the past few years, with the government aiming to achieve 500 GW of installed non-fossil-fuel capacity by 2030. According to government estimates, a total investment of about ₹42 trillion is needed to achieve this ambitious target.
The country plans to add 1,800 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2047 and 5,000GW by 2070, Mint reported in November. Industry executives say inorganic growth is the playbook in the energy space. According to KPMG, achieving growth over the next three years is the top operational priority for organizations as they pursue greater energy security, build digital infrastructure and scale renewables.
Some recent deals in the space include the Aditya Birla Group’s purchase of Sprng Energy from Shell for $1.8 billion in July 2026, Inox Clean Energy’s ₹6,000 crore buyout of Vena Energy India and a $750 million purchase of US solar assets from Boviet Solar. Inox also completed the acquisition of Vibrant Energy from Macquarie in April 2026.
Other players, including Avaada Electro, state-run NTPC Ltd's green energy arm NTPC Green Energy Ltd, Waaree Energies, Vikram Solar, ACME Solar, and Premier Energies, Inox Clean Energy, CleanMax, Juniper Energy, Hero Future Energies and SAE, are among those that have gone public in recent times, or are in various stages of their listing processes.

title: Paytm founder's Resilient Asset Management to sell up to 4.98% stake in fintech firm
content:
Indian fintech firm Paytm said on Monday that Netherlands-based Resilient Asset Management, fully owned by its founder and CEO Vijay Shekhar Sharma, has proposed to sell up to a 4.98% stake in the company.
Based on Paytm's last close, a sale of the 4.98% stake would be worth about 50.4 billion rupees ($527.71 million), according to Reuters calculations.
Local financial news outlet Moneycontrol reported, citing sources, that the floor price for the block trade has been set at 1,535.10 rupees per share, a discount of 2.9% to Paytm's last close on Monday.
This would value the stake sale at 48.95 billion rupees at the price, the outlet added. The company did not immediately respond to an email seeking details of the block trade.
Resilient acquired about a 10.20% stake in Paytm from Antfin(Netherlands) Holding B.V. in 2023 through optionally convertible debentures instead of a cash payment.
Under the deal, Resilient obtained ownership and voting rights attached to the shares, while Antfin retained the economic value.
Apart from Resilient's stake, Sharma directly owned a 9.03% stake in Paytm as of end-June, according to stock exchange data.
The proposed deal will not change Sharma's direct shareholding in the company, Paytm said.
Antfin will retain the value of the proceeds from the proposed block trade, the company added.
Paytm shares ended 1.4% lower at 1,580.20 rupees on Monday.

title: Tata Capital Healthcare Fund, Swiss impact investor bet on Tenet Diagnostics
content:
Tenet Diagnostics announced on Monday that it secured funding in a round led by healthcare-focussed private equity firm Tata Capital Healthcare Fund, as the diagnostics chain expands its footprint and services.
The Hyderabad-headquartered company, which offers radiology and pathology, raised $30 million (around Rs 287 crore) led by Tata Capital Healthcare Fund III and Swiss impact investor Blue Earth Capital, the company said in a statement. The two investors invested in Tenet Medcorp Pvt Ltd, which operates Tenet Diagnostics, for an undisclosed stake.
“The investment will help us accelerate our mission, deepen our footprint across India and bring reliable diagnostics to more communities who need it most,” said Sricharan Devineni, managing director, Tenet Diagnostics.
Veda Corporate Advisors acted as the exclusive financial advisor to Tenet Diagnostics on the deal.
The development was first reported by VCCircle. In May, Tata Capital Healthcare Fund was in the final stages of investing Rs 250-300 crore (around $26-32 million) in Tenet Diagnostics. Tenet was seeking a valuation of roughly Rs 1,000-1,200 crore (around $107-126 million) for the fundraise.
Tenet Diagnostics was founded in 2018 by Devineni. The company offers a wide spectrum of services across radiology, pathology and nuclear medicine with over 35 centres across 14 states, and over 3,000 super speciality tests. Its presence spans states such as Bihar, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh, in addition to its home state of Telangana.
“Diagnostics is increasingly becoming a consumer-driven category where patients value speed, transparency and accuracy. Under Sricharan’s leadership, Tenet has built one of the fastest-growing integrated diagnostics platforms in India, a model still rare at this scale," remarked Visalakshi Chandramouli, Managing Partner, Tata Capital Healthcare Fund.
Meanwhile, Tata Capital Healthcare Fund is also eyeing exits from companies in the diagnostics space. This includes Anderson Diagnostic in Chennai and Chandigarh-based Atulaya Healthcare, VCCircle reported in May.
Diagnostics has seen growing investor and strategic interest recently, with many viewing it as a consumer-driven category. Earlier this year, House of Diagnostics raised investment from asset manager 360 ONE Asset to scale up its diagnostics platform and expand its footprint in urban markets.
In April, PE-backed Redcliffe Labs also onboarded the World Bank's private sector investment arm, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) as a backer. Late last year, Vixar, formerly Arpwood Partners, acquired a controlling stake in Bengaluru-based dAlgnostiX Services Pvt Ltd.
 
The space is also seeing a wave of consolidations: GSK Velu's Neuberg is acquiring Mumbai-based NM Diagnostics and closing in on a New Delhi-based diagnostics chain, while Redcliffe Labs acquired Pune-based Megavision Diagnostics Center and Udaipur-headquartered Medicentre Sonography and Clinical Lab.
