title: Marico's acquired brands generate  ₹1,552 crore in FY26
content:
Fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) major Marico Ltd has assembled a sizeable portfolio of premium and digital brands through acquisitions over the past few years. Detailed subsidiary financials released with the Parachute-maker's annual report show the acquired businesses—Beardo, 4700BC, Cosmix, True Elements and Plix—generated a combined ₹1,552 crore in FY26 revenue. Marico reported consolidated revenue of ₹13,611 crore for the year. Profitability, however, remained uneven across the portfolio. Nutrition emerged as the standout category among the acquired businesses. Plix, the plant-based nutrition brand operated by Satiya Nutraceuticals, almost doubled its revenue to ₹864 crore in FY26 from ₹433 crore a year earlier. The surge helped drive a more than fivefold increase in profit to ₹25.9 crore from ₹4.77 crore. Marico first announced its investment in Plix in 2023, acquiring a 58% stake for ₹369 crore. It now owns 60% of the company. Cosmix also posted strong growth ahead of its acquisition by Marico. The functional nutrition brand reported revenue of ₹91.5 crore in FY26, compared with ₹47.25 crore in FY25, while profit doubled to ₹12.4 crore. Marico acquired a 60% stake in the company for ₹226 crore in February 2026. As Cosmix and 4700BC were acquired late in FY26, their performance is unlikely to have materially influenced Marico's FY26 consolidated financial results. Premium snacks brand 4700BC, operated by Zea Maize Pvt. Ltd., increased revenue 21% to ₹120 crore in FY26, but its loss widened 48% to ₹24 crore. Marico bought about 94% of the company for ₹227 crore in January 2026. HW Wellness Solutions Pvt. Ltd, which sells clean-label breakfast cereals, healthy snacks and millets under the True Elements brand, reported an 83% increase in loss to ₹43 crore in FY26, while revenue grew a modest 8%. Marico first invested in True Elements in 2022 and made it a wholly owned subsidiary in October 2025 after acquiring the remaining 46.02% stake for ₹138 crore. Men's grooming brand Beardo remained profitable. Zed Lifestyle, which operates Beardo, reported revenue of ₹299 crore and a profit of ₹22 crore in FY26. Marico first invested in the brand in 2017. Marico had also acquired Ayurvedic beauty brand Just Herbs in 2021. The business, operated by Apcos Naturals, has since been merged into the parent company. The subsidiary performance reflects a broader shift in Marico's portfolio strategy. Marico reported revenue of ₹13,611 crore in FY26, up 26% from the previous year, while recurring consolidated net profit after tax and minority interest rose 11% year-on-year to ₹1,762 crore. Premium and digital brands contributed 37% of revenue in FY26, up from 27% in FY20. The company aims to raise that share to 50% by FY30. Marico is targeting more than ₹15,000 crore in revenue in FY27 and, under its "Vision 2030" strategy, aims to reach ₹20,000 crore in revenue by 2030. Marico has accelerated acquisitions in recent years to sharpen its portfolio, adopting what it calls a "fewer, bigger, bolder and faster" approach while absorbing capabilities from younger consumer brands. “Data analytics, AI-led insights, and enhanced consumer engagement platforms are increasingly reshaping how we build brands, deepen personalisation and improve speed-to-market,” chairman Harsh Mariwala said in the annual report. Marico's Q4 investor presentation said its digital-first portfolio, including Beardo, Just Herbs, Plix and Kaya, crossed ₹1,100 crore in annualized revenue run rate (ARR) in FY26. “Marico’s digital-first portfolio is expected to achieve double-digit Ebitda margins by FY27 end, which should expand further to the teens by FY30,” analysts at Motilal Oswal Financial Services said in a 7 July report. On Thursday, shares of the company closed 2.43% higher on the National Stock Exchange at ₹860.55, compared with a 0.34% gain in the benchmark Nifty 50. Note: A previous version of this story incorrectly stated that Marico Ltd made ₹2,375 crore in revenue from operations from its newly acquired brands in FY26. The correct figure is ₹1,552 crore. The figures for Marico's latest acquisition, Cosmix, were also reported incorrectly. The brand's revenue from operations was ₹91.5 crore in FY26 and ₹47.25 crore in FY25; its profit after tax for FY26 was ₹12.4 crore. We regret the errors. title: Marico accelerates brand-building spends in Q1 as India volumes hit multi-quarter high
content:
New Delhi: Marico has accelerated its advertising and sales promotion investments in the first quarter of FY27, continuing its push behind core franchises and new growth engines after stepping up brand spends through FY26.
In its quarterly update for the period ended June 30, 2026, the company said, “ASP investments accelerated substantially as we invested in brand building initiatives to strengthen the long-term equity of our franchises and drive portfolio diversification.”
The company said consolidated revenue is expected to grow in the early twenties in Q1 FY27, driven by “robust broad-based performance across our core, digital and international businesses.”
In Q4 FY26, Marico’s advertising and sales promotion spends stood at Rs 320 crore, up 5% from Rs 305 crore in the same quarter of the previous year. For the full year FY26, the company’s advertising and sales promotion spends rose 15% to Rs 1,300 crore from Rs 1,128 crore in FY25.
The company had then said that it continued A&P investments despite significant input cost pressures.
The higher spending is tied to Marico’s attempt to protect the equity of established franchises such as Parachute, Saffola and Value Added Hair Oils, while scaling newer businesses in foods, premium personal care and digital-first brands.
“The India business further accelerated its growth trajectory, delivering double-digit underlying volume growth and reaching a multi-quarter high,” Marico said in the Q1 FY27 update.
Parachute Coconut Oil delivered double-digit volume growth, its highest in several quarters. The company said the brand’s performance reflected its “formidable equity, consumer trust and our sharp execution.”
Saffola Oils recorded mid-single-digit price-led revenue growth. However, volumes declined as Marico rationalised supply of select variants to maintain threshold profitability in the trade-off with volume growth.
Value Added Hair Oils delivered another strong quarter, with revenue growth in the twenties. The company said this was supported by “strategic focus on the mid and premium segments, enhanced direct reach driven by Project SETU and differentiated innovations.”
Foods and Premium Personal Care, including digital-first brands, continued to scale up in line with Marico’s aspirations, “reinforcing the acceleration of our diversification journey,” the company said.
Earlier in May, Marico entered the hair cleansing category with the launch of the Parachute Advansed Protein Shampoo range. The launch forms part of its broader strategy to expand into adjacent personal care categories and increase its presence in India’s shampoo market, which the company estimates to be worth more than Rs 10,000 crore.
When it comes to digital-first brands, the portfolio grew from an exit annual run rate of Rs 400 crore in Q3 FY24 to Rs 1,100 crore by the end of FY26, nearly tripling in about two years.
It includes Beardo, Just Herbs, True Elements, Plix, Cosmix and 4700BC, spanning men’s grooming, skincare, health foods, plant-based nutrition, functional wellness and premium snacking.
The company built this portfolio through a series of acquisitions and integrations. In Q1 FY26, Marico raised its stake in Plix to 60% on a fully diluted basis. In Q2 FY26, it acquired the remaining 46.02% stake in True Elements, making it a wholly owned subsidiary. Just Herbs was merged into Marico’s standalone operations in October 2025. In Q4 FY26, the company acquired a 94.02% stake in 4700BC and a 60% stake in Cosmix, both within the January-March 2026 quarter.
In FY26, revenue from operations stood at Rs 13,611 crore, up 26% year-on-year, the highest growth in 14 years. Its India business reported underlying volume growth of 8%, a seven-year high, while the international business delivered 20% constant currency growth, also a 14-year high.
In Q4 FY26, revenue from operations stood at Rs 3,333 crore, up 22% year-on-year.
The company had said at the time that e-commerce, including quick commerce, was the leading growth driver among channels, while traditional trade also showed visible improvement after consistent investments and targeted actions over two years.
Marico’s Foods portfolio crossed Rs 1,000 crore in revenues in FY26, while Premium Personal Care, including the digital-first portfolio, closed the year at around Rs 350 crore in revenues. The digital-first portfolio clocked an exit ARR of over Rs 1,100 crore.
In the international business, Marico said growth momentum remained strong, with mid-teens constant currency growth led by outperformance in Vietnam and MENA, along with positive contribution from other markets. Bangladesh saw a temporary moderation in growth due to pricing anniversarisation and marginal demand softness amid elevated inflation.
Input costs remained uneven during the quarter. The company said crude-linked derivatives and vegetable oils rose sharply. Copra prices corrected meaningfully, down around 45% from peak levels, although they remained above historical averages.
“Consequently, gross margin is expected to improve sequentially,” Marico said. “Overall, we expect a strong operating profit growth driven by robust business growth and softening in copra prices.”
The company said demand trends during the quarter remained steady, supported by resilient economic activity. It added that it remained optimistic about consumption trends while closely monitoring inflationary conditions and the impact of El Niño on the monsoon.
“The solid start to the year underscores strategic clarity, strength of our business model and execution rigour, reaffirming our confidence to achieve our full-year aspirations,” Marico said.
Marico said it maintained its medium-term aspiration of delivering sustainable and profitable volume-led growth, enabled by the strengthening brand equity of its core franchises and the scale-up of new growth engines across markets.

title: Pretoria High Court orders immediate return of Marico Chrome
content:
The Pretoria High Court on Thursday ruled that control of the Marico Chrome mine must immediately return to its lawful management, despite ongoing appeal attempts.
The dispute centres on Marico Chrome, a mine in the North West where the Bahurutshe Boo Manyana Traditional Community holds a 15% stake.
Judge Anthony Millar found that the Bahurutshe Boo Manyana Traditional Community had shown there were exceptional reasons for the earlier court order to take effect immediately while appeals continue.
Terminated legal authority
According to the judge, it would be unacceptable for the company to continue operating under people who no longer had legal authority.
This after court-appointed receivers Theodore Wilhelm van den Heever, Kgashane Christopher Monyela and Olckers Chopologe Koikanyang unlawfully remained in control of Marico Chrome Corporation after the company’s provisional liquidation was discharged on September 22, 2023.
The community argued it had been excluded from the company’s management since it was placed under provisional liquidation in 2016, even after that liquidation process ended.
The court agreed that the company should no longer be run by the former receivers, whose authority had already been terminated in an earlier judgement.
“What is at stake in the present matter is the proper and lawful governance of Marico Chrome,” Judge Millar said.
‘Community is a shareholder’
He added that the community, as a shareholder, had the right to appoint directors and participate in decisions affecting the company.
“The community is a shareholder. It is entitled to appoint directors to the board and to be represented in decisions affecting Marico Chrome.”
The judge said allowing the former receivers to remain in charge during a lengthy appeal process would effectively deprive the community of the relief it had already won.
“If the judgement is not put into operation, then it will be nothing more than the vacuous gesture posited in Incubeta.”
The court also criticised the continued operation of the company under individuals who were no longer legally authorised to manage it.
“I need not go into those. The fact that they are not lawfully entitled to deal with the affairs of Marico Chrome is enough.”
Misstatement of financial statements
Judge Millar found that Marico Chrome had continued to be managed by people who were neither directors nor liquidators after the provisional liquidation ended, while financial records continued to describe the company as being in liquidation.
“The continued misstatement of the financial statements of Marico Chrome as being in respect of a company in liquidation is to my mind sufficiently exceptional on its own.”
The judge also rejected claims that removing the receivers would cause serious disruption to the business.
“The receivers are not Marico Chrome. They are not its shareholders, nor its directors or its liquidators.”
He said any financial loss they might suffer could be compensated if they later succeeded on appeal.
Concluding his judgment, Judge Millar found that the community had proved it would suffer ongoing harm if the order was delayed, while the former receivers had failed to show they would face irreparable harm if it was enforced immediately.
“I find that the community has established exceptional circumstances and that they would suffer irreparable harm if the order sought is not granted.”
The ruling means the earlier court order remains in force while any appeals proceed.
The former receivers must hand over the company’s records and assets, stop acting on behalf of Marico Chrome, and allow the shareholders to restore the company’s lawful governance.
READ MORE: Community celebrates Marico Chrome victory amid fresh questions
- The Pretoria High Court ruled that control of Marico Chrome mine must return immediately to its lawful management despite ongoing appeals.
- The Bahurutshe Boo Manyana Traditional Community, holding a 15% stake, had been excluded from the mine’s management since provisional liquidation in 2016, which ended in September 2023.
- The court found the former receivers had no legal authority to operate the company after liquidation discharge and ordered their removal.
- Judge Millar emphasized the community’s right as a shareholder to appoint directors and participate in company decisions and ruled delaying enforcement would cause irreparable harm.
- The former receivers must hand over company records and assets, cease acting on behalf of Marico Chrome, ensuring restoration of lawful governance.

title: HUL names former Marico executive Koteshwar LN as Oziva CEO
content:
Special Coverage

Hindustan Unilever Ltd (HUL) has appointed Koteshwar L.N. as the new Chief Executive Officer of its wellness nutrition brand Oziva as the company intensifies its focus on the fast-growing health and wellbeing category.
The appointment comes months after HUL completed the acquisition of the remaining stake in Zywie Ventures, parent company of Oziva, making the wellness brand a wholly owned subsidiary. The FMCG major has identified health and wellbeing as a strategic growth area following the rise in consumer demand for nutrition, functional foods and preventive healthcare products.
Media reports indicate that he will report to Harman Dhillon, HUL’s Executive Director, Beauty & Wellbeing.
Executives familiar with the matter say that Koteshwar will take on responsibilities that extend beyond Oziva. He will also run HUL’s broader wellness portfolio including brands such as Liquid I.V., as the company looks to build a more integrated health and nutrition business.
Koteshwar has more than two decades of experience in FMCG, beverage and e-commerce verticals. He previously served in senior roles at Marico, including business and brand leadership. He has worked with Flipkart and The Coca-Cola Company, bringing experience in scaling consumer brands across multiple categories and channels.
The appointment comes as the wellness and nutrition space sees increasing competition. Consumer goods companies, digital-first start-ups and investors are increasingly taking bets on categories like protein supplements, plant-based nutrition, hydration products and preventive health solutions. Oziva began as a direct-to-consumer wellness brand and has now become one of the key assets in HUL’s health and wellbeing portfolio.
HUL’s first foray into Oziva came in 2023 when it acquired a 51% stake in Zywie Ventures. From there, the brand has grown rapidly. HUL’s annual report says Oziva grew to around ₹480 crore in revenues and saw a compound annual growth rate of almost 130% in two years after HUL’s investment.
HUL said in February 2026 that it was buying the remaining 49% in Zywie Ventures for ₹824 crore, adding that the wellness category is of strategic importance. Priya Nair, CEO and Managing Director, HUL, said at the time: “Health & wellbeing is an important growth vector for us, driven by growing consumer interest in everyday wellness. “With OZiva under our full ownership, we are doubling down on this exciting space to unlock the next phase of growth.”
As HUL deepens its presence in India’s fast-growing wellness nutrition market, the leadership transition is expected to support Oziva’s next phase of expansion.

"We confirm that Koteshwar LN has joined as the CEO of Oziva," HUL said in response to ET's email query. He will report to Harman Dhillon, HUL's executive director, beauty and well-being. According to an executive directly aware of the development, Koteshwar will also be in-charge of HUL's overall wellness portfolio which includes electrolyte drink Liquid I.V.
HUL, India's largest consumer company that makes a gamut of brands from detergents to cosmetics, completed the acquisition of Oziva, a plant-based clean-label consumer wellness brand through parent company Zywie in February. "Since entering the health and well-being category through the acquisition of a 51% stake in Zywie in 2023, the latter has scaled to about Rs 480 crore in two years at a CAGR of close to 130%," HUL said in its 2025-26 annual report.

title: Marico: How ‘Old FMCG Giant’ Is Trying to Become ‘Young’ Again and Reach ₹20,000 Cr in Revenue
content:
Synopsis: Marico is trying to move beyond its coconut oil and edible oil image by building new growth engines in foods, personal care and digital-first brands. The company wants to cross Rs. 20,000 crore revenue by FY30, but margins and execution remain key monitorables.
An old FMCG giant is trying to become relevant for a younger consumer base by moving beyond its traditional oil-led portfolio and building newer engines across foods, protein, beauty and digital-first brands. The idea is not to abandon its old cash-generating brands, but to use them as a base to fund the next phase of growth.
Marico Limited, the company behind brands such as Parachute, Saffola, Livon, Beardo, Plix, True Elements, 4700BC, Cosmix, Kaya and Just Herbs, ended FY26 with consolidated revenue of Rs. 13,611 crore, up 26 percent from Rs. 10,831 crore in FY25. EBITDA rose 9 percent to Rs. 2,328 crore, while recurring PAT increased 11 percent to Rs. 1,762 crore. However, EBITDA margin declined from 19.7 percent in FY25 to 17.1 percent in FY26, showing that the transformation is still being tested by input cost pressure.
The Old Marico Still Matters
The old Marico is built around highly trusted household brands. Parachute Coconut Oil, Saffola Edible Oils and Value Added Hair Oils remain the backbone of the India business. In Q4FY26, Parachute Coconut Oil contributed 36 percent of India revenues, Saffola Edible Oils contributed 17 percent and Value Added Hair Oils contributed 18 percent.
This legacy business is not weak. It is the reason Marico has pricing power, distribution strength and cash flow to invest in new categories. In FY26, India business volumes grew 8 percent, the highest in seven years, while India business revenue grew 28 percent. During Q4FY26, India business volume growth stood at 9 percent and revenue grew 21 percent.
Parachute remained resilient despite earlier pricing pressure. After adjusting for ml-age reductions, Parachute delivered low-single digit volume growth in Q4FY26. Copra prices corrected around 35 percent from peak levels, allowing selective pricing benefits to be passed on to consumers.
Value Added Hair Oils was one of the stronger pieces of the portfolio. The segment delivered robust growth in Q4FY26, supported by low-20s volume growth and market share gains. For the full year, the portfolio grew 20 percent, led by momentum in mid and premium segments outside Shanti Amla. Saffola Edible Oils remained steady, but the company continued to focus on threshold profitability instead of chasing every bit of volume.
Why Marico Wants To Become Younger
Coconut oil and edible oils are large, trusted and profitable categories, but they are also commodity-linked. In FY26, material cost as a percentage of revenue rose from 49.7 percent in FY25 to 55.5 percent. This is why EBITDA margin fell even though revenue growth was strong.
Marico wants to reduce the share of commodity-linked businesses from more than 70 percent to around 50 percent over a decade. That is the real meaning of the company trying to become “young” again. It wants a bigger part of revenue to come from categories where branding, innovation, digital reach and premium positioning matter more than raw material cycles.
This transformation is already visible. Foods and Premium Personal Care, including digital-first brands, now account for 23 percent of the India business. Marico expects this share to rise to about 27 percent in FY27 and eventually move to nearly one-third of India revenues by FY30.
The New Marico: Foods, Protein And Snacking
Foods is one of the biggest parts of Marico’s reinvention. The Foods portfolio crossed Rs. 1,000 crore revenue in FY26 and delivered 16 percent value growth in Q4FY26. Earlier, the company had paused growth in some areas to improve profitability, but it now expects to resume faster scale-up from FY27.
This portfolio is no longer just Saffola Oats. Marico now has a wider food basket covering mainstream health and wellness through Saffola, clean label breakfast and snacking through True Elements, premium gourmet snacking through 4700BC and functional nutrition through Cosmix and Plix.
The 4700BC acquisition gives Marico an entry into premium snacking. The brand is known for popcorn and has offerings such as popped chips, makhana, crunchy corn and nachos with avocado oil. Management earlier said the brand was clocking around Rs. 140 crore ARR and sees potential to scale its ARR three times over the next three years. Since 4700BC has limited retail presence today, Marico has room to use modern trade, e-commerce and distribution to widen the brand’s reach.
Cosmix gives Marico exposure to plant protein, gut-friendly nutrition, supplements and functional foods. Management earlier described it as a brand with proven D2C economics, Rs. 100 crore ARR and high-teen EBITDA margin. This is a very different customer from the traditional coconut oil buyer. It targets consumers who care about protein, wellness and cleaner labels.
True Elements gives Marico exposure to the clean-label breakfast and healthy snacking market and forms an important pillar of the company's food strategy. Management describes the brand as its platform for clean-label and modern breakfast and snacking products, complementing Saffola's mainstream health and wellness positioning.
Through categories such as muesli, granola, oats, nuts, seeds and healthier snacks, True Elements helps Marico target urban consumers who are becoming increasingly conscious about nutrition, ingredient quality and healthier lifestyles.
Premium Personal Care Is The Beauty Bet
The second major youth engine is Premium Personal Care. Marico is building this through brands such as Beardo for male grooming, Plix offers plant-based personal care, Kaya offers dermatologist backed solutions, Just Herbs for ayurveda inspired beauty, serums, male grooming and skincare. The portfolio comprising serums, male grooming and skincare exited FY26 at more than Rs. 350 crore ARR. The broader digital-first Premium Personal Care portfolio exited FY26 at more than Rs. 1,100 crore ARR.
Beauty and grooming categories are more suited to younger, digital consumers. They are influenced by social media, online reviews, quick commerce availability and product innovation. Marico’s core advertising spends are also shifting in that direction, with 55 percent now going towards digital media, while digital brands spend entirely on digital.
Management said it looks for product-market fit, category attractiveness, healthy unit economics, founder mentality and scalability. It is now targeting profitable brands with at least Rs. 100 crore to Rs. 150 crore scale, where Marico can use its platform to grow them faster.
Beardo and Plix are the proof points management keeps highlighting. Beardo has scaled five times after coming fully into Marico in 2020, while Plix has grown six times in two years. The company expects its digital-first portfolio to exit FY27 at double-digit EBITDA margin and reach teen EBITDA margins by FY30.
International Business Adds Another Growth Layer
Marico is also trying to become younger outside India. The international business delivered 20 percent constant currency growth in FY26, the highest in 14 years, while Q4FY26 growth stood at 19 percent. Bangladesh continued to remain strong, while Vietnam, South Africa and exports are becoming important growth engines. In Vietnam, the company is building a digital beauty and personal care play through brands such as Candid, Astroman and Lashe. Management said Candid, which forms roughly two-thirds of the Skinetiq business, is scaling in the science-based skincare segment with mid-premium positioning and mid-20s EBITDA.
Beyond Vietnam, Marico is also trying to replicate its digital-first playbook in the Middle East. Management highlighted markets such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia, which have some of the highest smartphone penetration rates globally. The company aims to build leadership in digital beauty and grooming across these markets, using the same model of premium brands, social commerce and digital-first consumer engagement that it is deploying in India and Vietnam.
The Road To FY30
Marico’s FY26 numbers show both strength and pressure. Margins remain the concern. Material cost rose 40 percent in FY26, much faster than revenue growth. EBITDA margin declined by 265 basis points for the full year and 114 basis points in Q4FY26. This shows that the company’s old commodity-linked structure still has a major influence on profitability.
For FY27, management expects high single-digit volume growth in India, mid-teen constant currency growth in international business, double-digit consolidated revenue growth, revenue crossing Rs. 15,000 crore and high-teen EBITDA growth, subject to stable macros. By FY30, the company aims to comfortably cross Rs. 20,000 crore revenue and aspire for mid-teen EBITDA growth.
Marico is not trying to become a completely new company. It is trying to make sure its old brands remain strong while new categories become large enough to change the growth profile. The legacy business gives stability, while foods, protein, snacking, beauty, grooming, digital brands and international premiumization are expected to bring youthfulness.
Commodity volatility, margin pressure, Saffola’s pricing environment and acquisition integration will remain key monitorables. If Marico executes well, the FY30 company may look very different from the coconut oil-led FMCG company investors have known for years.

title: Inside Marico's plan to win India's 80-90 crore consumers with a coconut-powered beauty ecosystem
content:
- FMCG
- 3 min read
Inside Marico's plan to win India's 80-90 crore consumers with a coconut-powered beauty ecosystem
                    Marico is making a major growth move by creating a coconut-based beauty range for millions of Indian consumers. The company has launched Parachute Advansed Protein Shampoo, entering the large shampoo market. This strategy targets the vast majority of India's population, aiming to deepen its presence beyond hair oils. The company believes in the growing consumer preference for natural ingredients.
                                    
            
        
                    
                    
                    
                                        Marico is making one of its biggest growth bets in recent years, not through premiumisation or niche innovation, but by building a complete coconut-led beauty ecosystem targeted at India's 80-90 crore mass consumers, Ashish Goupal, CEO – India Core Business, Marico Limited, told ETRetail.
The FMCG major has entered the Rs 10,000-crore shampoo category with the national launch of Parachute Advansed Protein Shampoo, marking one of the company's most significant category extensions.
"This is one of the most significant category extensions for our organisation. We realised there was no strong pan-India brand fulfilling the need for natural nourishment-driven cleansing solutions in the shampoo category," Goupal asserted.
But beyond the launch lies a much bigger ambition.
While many FMCG companies are chasing premium consumers, Marico is building for what Goupal calls the "large belly of India", the 80-90 crore consumers, spread across urban, semi-urban, and rural markets.
"India is growing in multiple ways. There is a digital India, and there is an emerging Bharat. All consumers are aspirational, but different brands need to talk to them differently. Parachute Advansed is a brand that talks to this 80-90 crore consumer base," he said.
The move gives Marico access to a category growing at 9-10 per cent annually while allowing it to deepen its presence beyond hair oils, which currently contribute nearly 50 per cent of Marico India's business.
"If you get success in this category, it can become a strong future growth engine for Marico," Goupal said.
The company is betting on a consumer shift towards natural ingredient-based beauty solutions, a trend it has already witnessed in international markets.
"When we scanned the market, we realised consumers globally are looking for solutions rooted in natural ingredients but backed by credibility. Coconut today is among the largest superfoods being talked about globally for hair and skin," he explained.
Marico's strategy is distinctly localised. While the South gets a coconut and shikakai variant, digital-first consumers will see rosemary-led offerings.
"We are witnessing a resurgence of regional beauty habits. That's why we are launching different ingredients for different markets. Shikakai has huge credibility in Southern India, while rosemary resonates strongly with modern e-commerce consumers," Goupal noted.
The company is launching eight-pack formats, ranging from a Re 1 sachet to 1.2-litre packs, ensuring accessibility across income segments.
"This is a mass launch because we want to fulfil the need for nourishment-based cleansing for the masses in India," he said.
Distribution will span general trade, modern trade, e-commerce, and quick commerce channels, leveraging Parachute Advansed's extensive nationwide network.
"Every outlet we have access to, whether rural or urban, tier I or tier IV, e-commerce or kirana, will have this product," Goupal said.
The launch also marks a shift in Parachute Advansed's evolution from a hair oil brand to a comprehensive beauty platform.
"We want to be a wholesome beauty brand driven by the nourishment of coconut. Today, we have hair oils, serums, masks, creams, and now protein shampoos and conditioners. We are building an entire hair-care regime under Parachute Advansed," he said.
Interestingly, Marico had already tested the shampoo proposition internationally before bringing it home. The company launched Parachute Advansed Shampoo in Bangladesh in 2021 and in the Middle East in 2023, where it has built a sizeable presence.
"We had the learning from international markets. Combined with consumer readiness in India and the growing relevance of coconut-based solutions, the timing felt right," Goupal said.
Despite inflationary pressures and global uncertainties, Marico remains focused on affordability-led growth rather than aggressive pricing.
"The best thing you can do in FMCG is invest in your brand and expand penetration. That's one reason we have launched with small packs and sachets, to ease consumer entry and adoption," he concluded.

title: Marico’s CMO on why Parachute Advansed shampoo is betting 55% of ad spends on digital
content:
For decades, if you asked an Indian household what Parachute Advansed meant, the answer would almost certainly involve a blue bottle of coconut oil. The brand, a flagship product of Marico Limited, has been embedded in the Indian hair care ritual for generations, with coconut oil as the foundation of healthy hair. But market dominance in the hair oiling segment only takes a brand so far.
India's shampoo market is now valued at over Rs 10,000 crore and is growing at 9 to 10% annually, according to Marico. It is a segment where Parachute Advansed, for all its equity in the pre-wash ritual, had no presence. That changed recently, as the company announced the launch of Parachute Advansed Protein Shampoo, its first foray into the cleansing category.
The range launches with eight variants across pack sizes from 80ml to 1.2L, with an entry-level Re. 1 sachet designed to drive trial. The lead variant pairs coconut milk with aloe vera, while the broader portfolio draws on ingredients like rosemary, amla, shikakai, and almond, each mapped to a specific consumer benefit.
Vikram Karwal, Chief Marketing Officer for India at Marico, explained what made this the right time to move. "Consumers are looking for trusted brands that deliver on their needs well. Consumers are also increasingly choosing products backed by nature," he said. "When it comes to the shampoo category, we saw this as an opportunity for Parachute Advansed. Armed with this understanding, we created a product that we believe will delight our consumers."
The positioning anchors on protein loss prevention, which Marico is using as the entry point into the damage repair segment. India's shampoo market has long been dominated by multinational companies. Entering on the strength of coconut equity alone would have been a soft pitch in a category that respects performance claims.
The launch arrives at an unusual moment. Geopolitical tensions linked to the West Asia conflict have created ripple effects across supply chains and consumer sentiment, with PM Modi calling for measured discretionary spending. Launching a new FMCG product into this environment, particularly a premium-positioned one, requires a clear rationale.
Karwal addressed this directly. "In an inflationary environment, the bigger players tend to benefit, and we believe that we are very well placed," he said. "We continue to invest behind our brands, which we believe will give us a comparative advantage over other players in the market. So this is not the time to pull the investment away."
It is a view backed by some evidence. During previous periods of economic stress, including the post-pandemic demand compression of 2020 to 2022, FMCG companies that maintained advertising investment recovered faster than those that pulled back. Marico's own revenue for FY25-26 reached Rs 136.1 billion. The logic Karwal outlines is that a downturn is precisely when the share of voice becomes more valuable, not less.
Reaching every corner, online and off
Marico has built a notably digital-heavy mix for this launch. Karwal noted that consumers are inquiring a lot on social media when it comes to their hair care requirements, their solutions, their problems and beauty needs, and that this has shaped where the brand is putting its money.
"We are going to invest heavily in the digital medium. Almost 55% of our advertising money is going to be spent on digital to make sure that we are able to engage with the new age consumers, give them the right information that they are seeking, and also collaborate with influencers to drive awareness and education around the products that we are launching," he said.
To meet consumers in those spaces, the company announced partnerships with over 3,000 content creators at the press conference. The strategy spans the full creator spectrum, from mega influencers to nano and hyperlocal creators in Tier II towns and rural markets. The explicit goal is last-mile reach, matching the geographic breadth that Parachute Advansed already commands in hair oil.
On commerce, the brand is investing in both general trade and e-commerce simultaneously. The Re. 1 sachet is squarely aimed at general trade penetration in smaller markets, while e-commerce consumers will have access to the full portfolio across all pack sizes. Quick commerce platforms, which have grown significantly in metro and Tier I cities, are part of the channel plan given the shift in how urban consumers discover and purchase personal care.
The target consumer, Karwal said, is deliberately broad. The brand wants to convert existing Parachute Advansed hair oil users into shampoo users within the same brand ecosystem, creating what he described as a complete hair care regime from pre-wash oiling to cleansing under a single brand.
“We want to have a meaningful play in the cleansing category," Karwal said when asked about business objectives over the next 12 to 24 months. "It is a big segment, it is 10,000 crore plus and evolving. We believe that we have the right equity and the right product to cater to consumers, which is meaningfully different and brings value to consumers."

title: Why Marico believes brands, AI and distribution will define FMCG’s next cycle
content:
- Exclusive
- Business of Brands
- 6 min read
Why Marico believes brands, AI and distribution will define FMCG’s next cycle
                    As AI reshapes product discovery and creators gain influence over purchase decisions, Marico is reworking its marketing and distribution strategy. The FMCG maker is increasing digital investments, expanding AI adoption across functions and targeting aspirational consumers in smaller towns, while continuing to invest in brands and distribution-led growth.
                                    
            
        Highlights
- AI is changing consumer behavior and product discovery.
- Digital media now exceeds 50 per cent of Marico's advertising spend.
- Influencer marketing is evolving to focus on real consumer experiences.
                    
                    
                    
                                        Artificial intelligence, creator-led influence and the growing aspirations of consumers in smaller towns will shape the next decade of consumer goods growth, according to Ashish Goupal, chief executive officer (CEO) – India Core Business, Marico, and Vikram Karwal, chief marketing officer, Marico, as the FMCG maker recalibrates its marketing and distribution playbook for a rapidly evolving consumer landscape.
The comments come as Marico expands the Parachute Advansed franchise into the shampoo category, but executives said the larger transformation underway is less about a single product launch and more about changes in how consumers discover products, consume media and make purchase decisions.
“Consumer discovery has moved from physical stores to search engines and is now increasingly becoming AI-assisted,” Goupal said. “We are focusing on areas where AI can create immediate value, consumer insights, communication development, productivity and process standardisation.”
AI moves from experimentation to execution
Marico is deploying AI across multiple functions, including consumer research, product development, content creation and internal operations. According to Goupal, the technology is already helping teams access insights faster and improve decision-making. He believes AI platforms are beginning to change information-seeking behaviour itself.
“People are increasingly using AI tools to synthesise information rather than relying only on traditional search,” he said.
Karwal said AI is also changing how marketing content is produced. Projects that previously required months of planning and execution can now be developed in significantly shorter timeframes using AI-enabled workflows.
“What traditionally took two to three months can now be completed in a matter of weeks,” Karwal said. “AI is helping improve both productivity and creative possibilities across content creation.”
The company is pursuing a hybrid model, combining in-house capabilities with agency partnerships to scale AI adoption across marketing and business functions. Despite growing adoption, both executives argued that AI will complement rather than replace marketers.
“Human judgment, relationships, experience and creativity remain critical,” Goupal said. “AI can improve efficiency, but decisions continue to require human intervention.”
Karwal added that while AI can support audience targeting, content adaptation and campaign optimisation, understanding consumer motivations and developing brand narratives remains a human responsibility.
Digital overtakes television in media mix
Changes in media consumption are also altering Marico’s advertising investments.
According to Goupal, digital media now accounts for over 50 per cent of Marico’s media expenditure, compared with around 30 per cent a few years ago. The shift reflects changing consumer behaviour as audiences increasingly divide their attention across social platforms, streaming services and creator-led content ecosystems.
Television, however, remains an important part of the mix because of its ability to deliver large-scale reach. “Digital helps create engagement and discoverability, while television continues to provide scale,” Goupal said.
For the recently launched shampoo brand, digital channels will account for approximately 55 per cent of campaign spending, according to Karwal. The campaign will involve collaborations with more than 3,000 creators across audience segments ranging from large national influencers to regional nano and pico creators.
Creator economy becomes central to brand building
Marico’s increasing reliance on creators reflects a broader shift in consumer trust and purchase behaviour. Consumers are increasingly seeking reviews, recommendations and demonstrations before trying new products, particularly in personal care categories.
“People want validation from users and creators before making purchase decisions,” Karwal said. “They want to hear experiences rather than only brand messages.”
According to Karwal, influencer marketing has evolved significantly over the past decade from endorsement-led campaigns to a recommendation-driven ecosystem, where consumers actively seek advice and product validation before making purchases. This behaviour is particularly pronounced in beauty and personal care categories, where consumers often look for demonstrations, reviews and real-life experiences before trying a new product.
Karwal said the company is deploying a tiered creator strategy spanning mega influencers to pico creators, supported by geographical targeting to improve relevance across markets and consumer segments.
The company views influencer marketing as an extension of consumer conversations rather than a replacement for traditional advertising.
“Consumers today don't just want to watch an advertisement. They want to understand how a product works, hear recommendations and participate in conversations around it,” Karwal said.
Television, digital media, influencer partnerships, outdoor advertising and commerce platforms are all expected to work together within an integrated media strategy.
Quick commerce and Brand investments
Marico also sees e-commerce and quick commerce as drivers of consumption rather than simply alternative sales channels. According to Goupal, rapid delivery services have reduced friction in replenishment cycles and increased purchase frequency across categories.
“Consumers no longer need to wait for the next shopping trip,” he said. “Products can be reordered instantly, which creates additional consumption opportunities.”
The rise of digital commerce has also improved product discoverability, particularly for new launches and category expansions, while providing brands with greater visibility into consumer behaviour.
Even as FMCG companies continue to face periodic inflationary pressures and input-cost fluctuations, Marico does not intend to reduce brand investments.
Goupal said strong brands become more important during periods of economic uncertainty and continue to be the company’s primary long-term asset.
“Brands are the foundation of the FMCG business,” he said. “Our approach is to continue investing behind them and drive penetration-led growth.”
The company’s investments are allocated based on expected returns and may vary depending on whether priorities involve established brands, innovation pipelines or new launches.
Marketers will need new skills
The increasing adoption of AI and digital tools is also changing expectations from marketing talent. According to Karwal, future marketers will need to combine traditional brand-building capabilities with technological adaptability.
“Understanding consumers, uncovering insights and building relevant propositions will remain fundamental skills,” he said. “But marketers will also need to navigate rapidly changing digital environments and use technologies such as AI with greater speed and precision.”
He added that the ability to combine marketing fundamentals with digital agility will become an important differentiator as media, commerce and consumer behaviour continue to evolve.
Distribution, aspiration and AI
Looking ahead, Marico believes competitive advantage in FMCG will increasingly come from a combination of brand building, distribution strength and technology adoption.
Goupal pointed to the growing importance of consumers in Tier-II and smaller markets, arguing that rising aspirations are reshaping demand across the country. “Consumers across smaller towns are exposed to the same brands, content and platforms as urban consumers,” he said. “The opportunity is increasingly driven by aspiration.”
He said companies with strong distribution capabilities will be best placed to serve that demand, while AI can help improve retailer connectivity, ordering systems and operational efficiency at scale.
Karwal said the pace of change across media, technology and consumer behaviour requires companies to continuously experiment and adapt. “The key is to move quickly, learn quickly and scale what works,” he said.

title: Stocks in news: Coal India, Marico, Fino Payments Bank, L&T, Physicswallah
content:
In today's trade, shares of Coal India, Marico, Fino Payments Bank, L&T, Physicswallah among others will be in focus due to various news developments.
Physicswallah, PC Jeweller, Swan Defence
Shares of Physicswallah, PC Jeweller and Swan Defence will be in focus as the companies will announce their fourth quarter results.
Brainbees Solutions
Brainbees Solutions narrowed its consolidated net losses to Rs 30.30 crore in the March-ended quarter versus Rs 77 crore in the year ago period, implying a 61% fall. The profit after tax (PAT) is attributable to the owners of the parent.
Coal India
Government of India will sell up to a 2% stake in Coal India Limited (CIL) through the offer for sale (OFS) route over May 27 and May 29, the state miner said on Tuesday in its filing to the exchanges. The floor price for the offer has been set at Rs 412 per equity share, a 10% discount from today's closing price of Rs 455.90 on the NSE.

Fino Payments Bank on Tuesday said the RBI has approved extension of tenure of Ketan Merchant as interim CEO for three months. In a stock exchange filing last week, Fino Payments Bank had said its board had approved extending the tenure of Merchant subject to regulatory approval.

Home-grown FMCG major Marico on Monday announced its entry into the hair cleansing segment by extending the coconut hair oil brand Parachute to the shampoo category. Through its Parachute 'Advansed Protein Shampoo', the Mariwala family promoted firm will compete in the hair cleansing (shampoo) segment.

Larsen & Toubro (L&T) on Tuesday said it has secured multiple orders in India, including a contract from JSW Utkal Steel Ltd and two projects from Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI).

title: Marico Launches Parachute Protein Shampoo Targeting Expansion In ₹30,000 Cr Hair Care Market
content:
Marico Launches Parachute Protein Shampoo Targeting Expansion In ₹30,000 Cr Hair Care Market
Marico diversifies its hair care portfolio with a protein-based shampoo, targeting the ₹30,000 crore hair cleansing market to reduce dependence on its core coconut oil business and capture premium retail consumers.
Market snapshot: Marico Limited has officially expanded its flagship Parachute franchise by launching the 'Parachute Advanced Protein Shampoo.' This move signals a deeper penetration into the high-margin hair cleansing segment, moving beyond its traditional dominance in the hair oil category to sustain long-term volume growth.
Data Snapshot
- Addressable Market: ₹30,000 Cr Hair Care segment in India.
- Marico Hair Oil Market Share: ~62% as of FY25.
- Target Category Growth: Shampoo segment growing at 8-10% annually.
- Product Positioning: Value-added protein-based cleansing.
What's Changed
- Product Diversification: From a market leader in hair oils to a more aggressive contender in the competitive shampoo category.
- Margin Mix: Shampoos generally offer higher gross margins (150-200 bps higher) compared to mass-market coconut oils.
- Strategic Pivot: Reducing the revenue concentration risk associated with copra price volatility by expanding the value-added hair care portfolio.
Key Takeaways
- Leveraging Brand Equity: Utilizing the trusted 'Parachute' brand to enter the cleansing category reduces customer acquisition costs.
- Growth Strategy: Aligns with Marico's goal to achieve 12-15% revenue growth through premiumization.
- Distribution Advantage: The product will benefit from Marico's existing 5.5 million retail touchpoints across India.
SAHI Perspective
Marico's entry into the protein shampoo sub-segment is a calculated move to challenge incumbents like HUL and P&G. By branding it under Parachute Advanced, they are bridging the gap between traditional care (oils) and modern regimes (cleansing). From a financial perspective, this improves the quality of earnings by pivoting toward non-commodity linked products, which provides a buffer against fluctuating copra costs.
Market Implications
The launch is likely to be viewed positively by institutional investors as it addresses the 'single-product dependence' narrative. The capital allocation toward the hair cleansing segment suggests a shift in marketing spend toward high-frequency, urban-centric categories. Sector-wide, it intensifies competition in the FMCG personal care space, potentially leading to increased ad-spends by rivals.
Trading Signals
Market Bias: Bullish
Expansion into high-margin segments and a stable demand outlook for the Parachute brand support a positive bias. Volume growth in diversified categories is expected to offset any sluggishness in rural mass-market oils.
Overweight: FMCG, Personal Care, Consumption
Underweight: Commodity-linked Staples
Trigger Factors:
- Market share gains in the shampoo category over the next two quarters.
- Stability in copra raw material costs.
- Q1FY27 volume growth trajectory.
Time Horizon: Medium-term (3-12 months)
Industry Context
The Indian hair care market is undergoing a structural shift toward problem-solving products (anti-dandruff, protein-rich, hair-fall control). While the hair oil market is mature, the shampoo and post-wash segment continues to see high double-digit growth in urban centers, driven by increased grooming awareness and premiumization.
Key Risks to Watch
- Intense competition from established players like Sunsilk, Dove, and Head & Shoulders.
- High initial marketing and sampling costs which may depress near-term margins.
- Potential cannibalization or brand dilution if not positioned distinctly from the oil category.
Recent Developments
In the last 90 days, Marico reported a consolidated revenue growth of 7%, led by international business performance. The company also announced a strategic investment in a digital-first skincare brand to bolster its 'One Marico' ecosystem. Additionally, rural demand recovery has shown early signs of a 3% volume uptick in the January-March quarter.
Closing Insight
Marico’s expansion into the shampoo category is not just a product launch; it is a structural play to evolve into a complete personal care powerhouse. Success in this category could re-rate the stock's P/E multiple as the revenue mix shifts toward premium hair care.
FAQs
Why is Marico launching a shampoo under the Parachute brand?
Parachute has over 60% market share in hair oils and high brand trust. Using this brand equity allows Marico to enter the ₹30,000 crore shampoo market with lower marketing hurdles compared to a new brand.
How does this launch affect Marico's profit margins?
Shampoos generally offer better margins than plain coconut oil. This shift toward value-added products helps Marico maintain its 20-22% EBITDA margin guidance even when raw material prices like copra fluctuate.
What does this mean for retail consumers?
Consumers get access to a protein-fortified cleansing product from a trusted traditional brand. It provides an integrated hair-care solution (oil + shampoo) within the same brand ecosystem.

title: Marico’s CEO Saugata Gupta bets on building the next digital-first brands from within
content:
Special Coverage
“Range matters now”: Microsoft’s Puneet Chandok, GrowthSchool’s Vaibhav Sisinty on the skills that will define Gen Z careers
As legacy FMCG companies grapple with rapidly shifting consumer behavior, Marico is increasingly looking inward to build the next generation of digital-first brands rather than relying solely on acquisitions. Speaking to Storyboard18's editor Delshad Irani, Marico MD and CEO Saugata Gupta said the company’s journey into D2C and digital-native businesses has fundamentally reshaped how it thinks about innovation, speed, experimentation and even organizational structure.
“What we have learnt is the high-velocity evolution of these businesses — build fast, start small, scale faster and fail faster,” Gupta said, reflecting on Marico’s experience with a series of digital-first acquisitions across food, wellness and personal care.
Over the last few years, Marico has emerged as one of India’s more aggressive traditional FMCG players in the digital-native space, acquiring and investing in brands such as Plix, Beardo and other emerging businesses across categories. But Gupta suggested the company’s ambitions are now moving beyond acquisitions toward internally incubating new-age brands.
“The challenge for my team now is: after having done six acquisitions, can we start creating brands organically in the same way?” he said.
“Our legacy model is built on scale, mass distribution and efficiency,” he said. “Digital-native brands operate differently.”
Unlike legacy FMCG businesses that often prioritize scale from the outset, digital-first ventures thrive on rapid experimentation, niche communities and agile product development. Gupta said one of Marico’s biggest realizations was accepting that traditional companies do not necessarily “know it all” when entering the D2C ecosystem.
That thinking has informed Marico’s acquisition strategy as well. Rather than immediately absorbing founders and brands into the larger corporate structure, Marico typically acquires a majority stake while allowing founders to independently run the business for a few years before integration.
“We use those years to learn,” Gupta said.
According to Gupta, one of the most valuable lessons from digital-native founders has been their willingness to take risks that larger organizations often hesitate to embrace.
Citing wellness brand Plix as an example, Gupta said the company leaned heavily into plant-based positioning and newer consumer narratives that a traditional FMCG company may once have viewed as risky or niche.
“Founders are naturally far more experimental,” he said. “Their risk-taking ability is much higher.”
At the same time, Gupta argued that Marico’s scale gives these startups operational stability. Supply chain support, procurement strength and access to capital free founders from day-to-day survival pressures and allow them to focus on product innovation and consumer engagement.
The company is already beginning to apply those learnings internally.
Gupta revealed that Marico has started experimenting with building digital-first brands from within the organization across international and domestic markets. In Vietnam, the company has already launched newer digitally driven brands, while in India it is piloting digitally native, model-led businesses aimed at younger consumers.
But Gupta admitted that incubating such businesses within a large FMCG company comes with structural challenges.
“It’s very difficult for the same marketing team to manage one large legacy brand and also manage a digital-native startup mindset,” he said, adding that these businesses require different capabilities, operating rhythms and cultural orientations.
That difference is particularly visible in how new-age brands approach marketing and communication.
Gupta said traditional marketers often begin with a polished television commercial and then adapt the campaign for digital platforms. In contrast, digital-native brands increasingly start with creators, communities, short-form content and social engagement before scaling the narrative elsewhere.
He also highlighted the growing role of social commerce and influencer ecosystems, particularly in markets like the Middle East and Vietnam, where creator-led shopping behavior is accelerating far faster than in traditional retail environments.
“There’s huge social commerce there,” Gupta said.
At Marico, that has translated into a far more content-heavy operating model. Gupta said the company now produces thousands of pieces of digital content and has significantly expanded its capabilities around analytics, creator engagement and digital storytelling.
Artificial intelligence is also beginning to play a larger role in the company’s innovation and marketing processes. He believes the broader marketing ecosystem is still only “halfway there” in understanding the implications of AI-led creativity and automation.
Still, despite all the disruption, Gupta insisted that the fundamentals of brand building remain unchanged.
“Understanding unmet consumer needs and investing behind brand building still matter,” he said. “The communication format may change, but the core principles don’t.”
He also warned against becoming overly dependent on performance marketing and discount-led growth — a trap he believes many digital-first brands risk falling into.
“It’s very tempting to spend everything on performance marketing because it gives quick results,” Gupta said. “But long-term brand building requires patience.”
As a result, Marico has begun pushing even its digital-native businesses to allocate greater spending toward top-of-funnel storytelling and long-term equity creation rather than relying exclusively on conversion-focused marketing.
For Gupta, the next phase of FMCG growth will likely belong to companies that can combine the agility of startups with the scale advantages of legacy businesses. And increasingly, Marico appears determined to prove it can do both.

Rather than treating Gen Z as a uniform consumer segment, marketers are increasingly having to account for individual behaviours, fragmented content consumption and a stronger expectation

title: Exclusive: Marico CEO Saugata Gupta on Gen Z, digital disruption and why “marketing is the most disrupted function”
content:
Special Coverage
“Range matters now”: Microsoft’s Puneet Chandok, GrowthSchool’s Vaibhav Sisinty on the skills that will define Gen Z careers
As the FMCG landscape undergoes one of its biggest transformations in decades, legacy companies are being forced to rethink everything from brand building and media strategy to innovation cycles and consumer engagement. Few leaders have navigated this shift as aggressively as Marico MD and CEO Saugata Gupta, who has pushed the company deeper into digital-first brands and new-age consumer businesses while continuing to scale legacy powerhouses like Parachute and Saffola.
In this exclusive conversation with Storyboard18’s editor Delshad Irani, Gupta reflects on the evolution of marketing from the television era to today’s fragmented consumer journeys, the rise of Gen Z, the creator economy, AI-led efficiencies and why marketers must learn to operate across every format — from performance marketing to iconic television storytelling.
Edited excerpts.
Q. Marico has been one of the standout FMCG companies when it comes to embracing DTC and digital-first brands early. From your perspective, how has brand building fundamentally evolved over the years?
Today, everything has changed. If you ask me, marketing is probably the most disrupted function in FMCG. Consumers — especially Gen Z — make choices very differently now. Earlier, consumers largely consumed what they were told to consume. Today, discovery, influence, persuasion and purchase all happen across different touchpoints. Someone may discover a brand on social media, evaluate it somewhere else and finally purchase it either online or offline. The journey is no longer linear.
At the same time, entry barriers have collapsed because of e-commerce and quick commerce. Earlier, brands could dominate categories for decades. Today, any successful idea can be replicated within six months. So agility and innovation are critical.
That said, personal care and food behave differently. Food is far more “flirtatious” — consumers experiment more. Personal care still enjoys relatively stronger loyalty. But across categories, marketing today demands constant adaptation.
Q. You’ve also been vocal about Marico becoming more digital-first. How do you see the media shift playing out? Is television becoming less important?
I don’t think media consumption is shrinking. India still has among the cheapest data rates globally, and consumers are consuming enormous amounts of content. Television remains effective, especially for large-scale brands.
But the media mix is definitely changing. For example, in some of our newer or premium categories, nearly 70% of our media spends are digital. In some international markets like Vietnam, we run certain brands almost entirely digitally. That works because the objective is about reaching the right consumers efficiently.
For truly large brands, television still matters. But for premium personal care or food brands, digital-first approaches can absolutely work.
Q. Marico sits at the intersection of legacy FMCG and digital-native brands. What have you had to unlearn while building and acquiring these businesses?
One of the biggest realizations has been accepting that we don’t know everything. Traditional FMCG models are built around scale, mass distribution and efficiency. Digital-first brands operate very differently.
That’s why our acquisition model is structured the way it is. We typically take a majority stake, allow founders to continue running the brands for a couple of years and learn from them before integrating. Those years become our learning phase.
The biggest learning has been speed — building fast, testing fast and scaling fast. The second has been understanding influencer ecosystems and social commerce. In markets like the Middle East and Vietnam, social commerce is huge.
But some fundamentals haven’t changed: understanding consumer needs and investing behind brand building. What has changed is the format of communication. Earlier, marketers would start with a 30-second TV commercial. Today, you often begin with digital-first content and build outward from there.
Q. What have you personally learnt from interacting with founders of these digital-first brands?
Founders tend to have a very strong “built to last” mindset. The good founders are deeply clear about what their brands stand for. They’re willing to take risks that large traditional companies often hesitate to take.
For example, with a brand like Plix, we leaned into plant-based positioning in a serious way. Traditional FMCG companies might have found that too risky earlier. Founders are naturally more experimental.
What Marico brings to the table is operational capability — procurement, supply chain, funding and scale. That frees founders to focus on innovation and the next big idea.
Q. You’ve consistently argued against cutting marketing spends even during difficult periods. What’s your philosophy there?
Over the last several quarters, we have not cut back on brand investments. We operate across multiple emerging markets, and in these markets, long-term growth has to be volume-led. Inflation may help temporarily, but sustainable growth comes from driving volumes and strengthening brands.
The two things we do not compromise on are investing in long-term capabilities and investing in brand equity. Tough times are actually opportunities to become more efficient.
What I tell teams is: if you need to reduce spends, don’t cut your strongest bets. Cut the bottom 2% — the things that are not working. Don’t become democratic about cuts and weaken your strongest brands.
Q. You’ve also raised concerns around overdependence on performance marketing. Why?
Because it’s very tempting. Performance marketing gives quick results. Discounting helps e-commerce growth. But long-term brand building requires patience.
I actively push our digital ventures to spend a minimum amount on top-of-funnel brand building and not just focus on performance metrics. Otherwise, you risk creating businesses that grow fast temporarily but don’t build enduring equity.
Q. How do you keep legacy brands like Parachute relevant for younger consumers?
The key is continuous innovation and contemporary relevance. Take Parachute Advansed — the challenge is not necessarily increasing penetration but making the category contemporary for younger consumers.
That means introducing new formats, new ingredients and more solution-oriented products. Consumers today are looking for convenience and functionality. Whether it’s hair masks, onion oil or newer hair-care formats, the idea is to keep evolving the proposition while staying true to the core benefit.
Q. What’s Marico’s approach to creators and influencer-led storytelling?
Creators are absolutely important, and we work with a large number of them across our digital brands. But we focus heavily on authenticity and impact rather than just scale.
If influencer marketing becomes excessive or inauthentic, it can damage trust. And trust is foundational for FMCG brands. That’s why authenticity matters enormously.
Q. Do you believe traditional advertising creativity has weakened in the digital era?
No, not at all. Great storytelling still matters. A great 30-second commercial still works — even on platforms like YouTube.
The difference is that marketers today need to master every format. I often use a cricket analogy: great T20 players still require a strong Test cricket foundation. Similarly, great marketers today must understand performance marketing, influencer marketing and classic brand storytelling together.
The fundamentals of marketing haven’t changed. Understanding consumers remains the most important thing.
Q. You’ve spoken a lot about curiosity. How have you managed to retain that as a leader?
I believe you can learn from anyone. The day you think you know everything is the day decline begins. Intellectual arrogance is one of the biggest enemies of any company. Arrogance and complacency eventually lead to downfall.
At Marico, we actively encourage humility and learning. We even ask leaders to reflect on how often they say, “I don’t know,” or “I made a mistake.” As long as you retain that mindset, you continue evolving.

	Among individual stocks, Vijaya Diagnostic Centre surged 8 per cent to ₹1,375. The stock was quoting higher for the eight straight trading day, soaring 25 per cent during the period.
 
	The company delivered strong numbers for the March 2026 quarter (Q4FY26) with revenue/EBITDA/PAT growing 27 per cent/39 per cent/38 per cent YoY beating estimates by 5 per cent/10 per cent/7 per cent, respectively, analysts at JM Financial Institutional Securities said.

	In FY26, Vijaya delivered 19.5 per cent growth, ahead of its 15 per cent guidance. This marks the third consecutive year of outperformance. While the company maintains its guidance, analysts believe strong momentum persists in the diagnostics space, fuelled by consumer consolidation towards organised offline players, the return of B2B business and upscaling of packages. 	Shares of Tata Consumer Products soared 7 per cent to ₹1,262 in intra-day trade. In the past one month, the stock has rallied 15 per cent, as compared to 0.45 per cent decline in the Nifty 50.

Growth businesses continue to scale up strongly led by Tata Sampann and Tata Soulfull, while Capital Foods is expected to return to a strong growth trajectory in FY27, ICICI Securities said in a note.
	Organic business is expected to sustain 25-30 per cent growth, supporting 30 per cent growth in the overall growth portfolio and continued double-digit consolidated revenue growth in FY27. Tea prices are expected to remain benign while coffee prices are likely to decline from Q1FY27 and also as lower-cost inventory flows in the international business, supporting margin improvement across India tea and US coffee businesses. Overall EBITDA margins are expected to expand by 50-75bps in FY27. The brokerage firm expects Tata Consumer Products revenues/EBITDA/Adjusted PAT to grow at a CAGR of 13 per cent/19 per cent/21 per cent over FY26-28E.
	Meanwhile, share price of Laurus Labs hit a new high of ₹1,274.50, gaining 4 per cent on the NSE in intra-day trade. In the past one week, the stock rallied 9 per cent as the company sustained strong operating performance for the Q4FY26. In comparison, the Nifty 50 was down 1 per cent.

title: Marico: 9 Acquisitions in 9 Years - How the Company Is Silently Building Its FMCG Leadership
content:
Synopsis: While traditional FMCG growth remains steady, Marico is quietly building its next leg through acquisitions. With a growing portfolio of digital-first, premium brands, the company is no longer just an FMCG player; it is becoming a platform that identifies, funds, and scales the next generation of consumer brands.
For years, this FMCG company was known for its strong core brands and consistent execution in categories like hair oils and packaged foods. That base continues to deliver, but the real shift is happening elsewhere. Instead of relying solely on organic growth, the company is aggressively expanding through acquisitions, with over 9 deals in recent years, targeting niche, high-growth consumer brands. This is not a one-off strategy; it is becoming central to how the company plans to grow.
With a market capitalisation of ₹1,07,759 crores, the shares of Marico Limited are trading at ₹830 apiece in today's market session, down 0.23% from its previous day close of ₹832. The stock is nearing its 52-week high of ₹843, showing a decent run-up.
Recent Performance
Marico reported a 22% year-on-year rise in consolidated revenue from operations to ₹3,333 crore for Q4 FY26, while net profit grew 14% to ₹408 crore. EBITDA rose 14% to ₹521 crore, though margins dipped slightly to 15.6% from 16.8% a year ago.
For FY27, the company is targeting double-digit topline growth to surpass ₹15,000 crore, backed by high single-digit volume growth in India, and the board has also proposed a final dividend of ₹4 per share, with a record date of July 30, 2026.
The Shift from Organic Growth to Strategic Expansion
For years, Marico was known for Parachute and Saffola. Predictable, consistent, and deeply entrenched in Indian households. That base continues to perform. But the company has quietly been running a parallel strategy, one built around acquisitions rather than organic brand building.
Since 2017, Marico has steadily built its digital-first portfolio through nine acquisitions, starting with Beardo in men's grooming, followed by Just Herbs in Ayurvedic beauty, True Elements in healthy snacking, Purité de Provence and Liv in premium beauty, and Plix in plant-based nutrition.
The acquisition logic is consistent across each deal. Marico targets brands that already have product-market fit, a profitable or near-profitable operating model, and a strong digital community, then uses its own distribution, supply chain, and capital to scale them faster than they could independently. However, the company practices a founder-managed style of acquisition, where it does not acquire 100% of the stake in almost all deals, and retains the founder
The pace accelerated sharply in early 2026 with three deals closed in three weeks: a gourmet popcorn brand 4700BC for ₹226.8 crore, a plant-based protein startup Cosmix for ₹226 crore, and a Vietnamese skincare company Skinetiq for ₹261.6 crore.
The Numbers Behind the Strategy
Marico's digital business is targeting ₹1,000 crore in annual revenue run rate by the end of FY26, and by 2030, the management projected that Marico's digital portfolio could collectively generate Rs 4,000 crore in revenue by FY30.
The core business, meanwhile, is not being neglected. For FY26, the total sales of the company stood at ₹13,611 crores. The dividend of ₹4 per share signals balance sheet confidence. The core funds the acquisitions. The acquisitions drive the re-rating.
Execution Is Where the Thesis Gets Tested
The risks are real and worth flagging. Integrating multiple brands without diluting what made them work is genuinely difficult. Founder-led, digitally native businesses operate very differently from legacy FMCG portfolios, and that tension does not disappear after an acquisition closes. Management bandwidth across a growing number of simultaneous integrations is a real constraint that does not show up in quarterly numbers until it does.
The phased acquisition model, buying majority stakes with options to acquire the rest later, limits downside but means the full benefit of successful brands takes time to flow through to consolidated earnings.
Not every bet will pay off, and scaling brands to meaningful revenue contribution is a different challenge from identifying and acquiring them in the first place, and the portfolio has become more complex.
Market Takeaway
Marico is running two businesses simultaneously. The first is the legacy FMCG operation, stable, cash-generative, and still growing. The second is a brand-building platform that acquires, scales, and potentially exits consumer brands across beauty, wellness, and food. If executed well, the company could transition from being a traditional FMCG player to a platform that creates and scales brands.
The real question is not whether these brands can grow, but whether Marico can consistently pick winners. Because in the next phase of FMCG, the edge may not lie in distribution alone, but in the ability to identify what consumers will want next.

title: Marico Promoter Group Files No-Encumbrance Declaration for FY26 Under SEBI Takeover Regulations
content:
Marico Promoter Group Files No-Encumbrance Declaration for FY26 Under SEBI Takeover Regulations
Harsh Mariwala filed a declaration under Regulation 31(4) of the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeover) Regulations, 2011, on April 3, 2026, on behalf of Marico Limited's promoter group and PAC. The declaration confirms that no encumbrance — direct or indirect — was placed on promoter shares during the financial year ended March 31, 2026, beyond previously disclosed instances. The annexure lists 33 members of the promoter and promoter group as on March 31, 2026. Additionally, shares held by the late Mr. Kishore V Mariwala were transmitted to Ms. Anjali R Mariwala and Ms. Paula R Mariwala on February 24, 2026, following probate of his Will.
*this image is generated using AI for illustrative purposes only.
Harsh Mariwala, on behalf of himself, other promoters, and members of the promoter group along with Persons Acting in Concert (PAC) of Marico Limited, has submitted a formal declaration to the stock exchanges dated April 3, 2026. The declaration was filed under Regulation 31(4) of the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeover) Regulations, 2011, confirming that no encumbrance — whether direct or indirect — was created on the shares of Marico Limited held by the promoter group during the financial year ended March 31, 2026, except for those already disclosed previously.
Declaration Details
The declaration was digitally signed by Harsh Charandas Mariwala on April 3, 2026, and submitted to both BSE Limited and the National Stock Exchange of India Limited. The filing reaffirms the promoter group's compliance with SEBI's shareholding disclosure norms for FY26.
Promoter and Promoter Group Composition
The annexure accompanying the declaration lists 33 individuals, entities, and trusts forming the promoter and promoter group as on March 31, 2026. The composition includes direct promoters as well as an extensive promoter group comprising family members, family trusts, and related entities.
Note on Share Transmission
The filing includes an important note regarding a change in the promoter group composition. Subsequent to the demise of Mr. Kishore V Mariwala, a promoter of the company, the equity shares held by him in his individual capacity were transmitted to Ms. Anjali R Mariwala and Ms. Paula R Mariwala — both members of the promoter group — on February 24, 2026. This transmission was carried out in accordance with the Will probated by the Hon'ble High Court. Accordingly, in line with the Master Circulars issued by the National Stock Exchange of India Limited and BSE Limited, the name of Late Mr. Kishore V Mariwala has been excluded from the list of Promoter/Promoter Group.
